title: Effects of blood flow restriction training in adult upper-limb musculoskeletal rehabilitation: A systematic review.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Blood flow restriction training (BFRT) has been proposed as a low-load rehabilitation strategy for symptomatic and postoperative upper-limb musculoskeletal conditions. This review evaluated the clinical effects, tolerability, and prescription characteristics of BFRT in adult upper-limb musculoskeletal rehabilitation.
METHODS: This systematic review was registered in International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (CRD420261299726) and reported with reference to Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses 2020. CENTRAL/Cochrane Library, Embase via Ovid, MEDLINE/PubMed, Science Citation Index/Web of Science, and Scopus were searched without a start-date restriction before February 18, 2026; backward reference-list/citation checking was also used. Randomized trials, case series, and case reports were eligible. Findings were synthesized narratively because of heterogeneity, and studies were appraised using risk of bias 2 or design-appropriate Joanna Briggs Institute checklists.
RESULTS: Twenty reports were included: 9 parallel-group randomized trials, 1 randomized crossover trial, 2 case series, and 8 case-report publications. Across the reports, 340 participants were enrolled or randomized and 326 contributed to the analyzed/treated clinical samples; 158 were men (48.5%) and 168 were women (51.5%). In a sham-controlled lateral elbow tendinopathy trial, BFRT resulted in a significantly greater reduction in 12-week pain (between-group difference -1.54, 95% confidence interval [CI] -2.89 to -0.18; P = .026) and patient-rated tennis elbow evaluation (PRTEE) (-15.23, 95% CI -23.57 to -6.90; P < .001). In patients with chronic lateral epicondylitis, PRTEE reduction (-24.20 ± 4.02 vs -15.60 ± 3.71; P = .001) and quick disabilities of the arm, shoulder and hand reduction (-12.83 ± 4.97 vs -7.51 ± 4.72; P = .025) were significantly greater with BFRT plus conventional therapy, whereas between-group pain and strength changes were not significant. In nonoperative distal-radius-fracture rehabilitation, mean activity-pain reduction was 4.0 versus 2.3 points (P = .03). In rotator-cuff tendinopathy, BFRT resulted in significantly greater biceps thickness (P = .002) and internal-rotation strength (P = .040). Conversely, a pragmatic elbow trial found no significant between-group difference in 12-month PRTEE (adjusted contrast + 4.32, 95% CI -9.17 to 17.81; P = .53).
CONCLUSION: BFRT may be considered a low-load adjunct in adult upper-limb musculoskeletal rehabilitation settings, but it is not consistently superior to active rehabilitation for pain, strength, or function. Confidence remains limited by small samples, heterogeneous prescriptions and co-interventions, uncontrolled designs, and incomplete adverse-event ascertainment.

title: Clinical Pathway Management for Platelet-Rich Plasma Therapy in Kellgren-Lawrence Grade I and II Knee Osteoarthritis: A Prospective, Multicenter, Double-Blind Randomized Controlled Trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Clinical outcomes after platelet-rich plasma (PRP) treatment for knee osteoarthritis are inconsistent, and some well-designed trials show no benefit. Whether a standardized multicomponent pathway improves outcomes relative to conventional PRP care is uncertain.
PURPOSE: To compare the efficacy, safety, satisfaction, and costs of a standardized PRP pathway versus physician-directed conventional PRP care in Kellgren-Lawrence grade I and II knee osteoarthritis.
STUDY DESIGN: Randomized controlled trial; Level of evidence, 1.
METHODS: At 3 hospitals, 240 patients were randomized 1:1 to a standardized PRP clinical pathway (PRP-CP; n = 120) or physician-directed conventional PRP care (PRP-C; n = 120). PRP-CP combined standardized selection, quality-controlled leukocyte-poor PRP, ultrasound-guided injections, staged rehabilitation, and systematic follow-up. Primary 12-month outcomes were visual analog scale (VAS) pain, Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC) total, and International Knee Documentation Committee (IKDC) scores; secondary outcomes included achievement of the minimal clinically important difference, satisfaction, adverse events, and costs.
RESULTS: At 12 months, PRP-CP produced greater changes than PRP-C in VAS (mean difference [MD], -2.98 [95% CI, -3.64 to -2.32]), WOMAC total (MD, -8.63 [95% CI, -11.35 to -5.90]), and IKDC (MD, 10.25 [95% CI, 8.37 to 12.13]) scores (all P < .001). Achievement of the minimal clinically important difference favored PRP-CP at 3, 6, and 12 months for the VAS and at 6 and 12 months for the IKDC and WOMAC (P < .05). Satisfaction was greater with PRP-CP (odds ratio, 1.79 [95% CI, 1.11-2.89]; P = .017). An adverse event occurred in 17 of 115 patients in the PRP-CP group (14.8%) versus 36 of 113 patients in the PRP-C group (31.9%) (Fisher exact test: P = .003). Mean costs were CN¥15,199.9 versus CN¥14,754.4, respectively; the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio was CN¥66.0 per WOMAC point. Effects were generally consistent across centers, and blinding was maintained.
CONCLUSION: The standardized multicomponent pathway produced greater 12-month improvements in pain and function than conventional PRP care, with fewer adverse events. Because components were bundled and no placebo group was included, the trial does not establish PRP efficacy or component-specific effects.

title: Physical activity levels two years after total knee arthroplasty and preoperative patient characteristics: a secondary analysis of the MOVE randomized controlled trial.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: At one year after total knee arthroplasty (TKA), patients are less physically active than age-matched peers, but physical activity (PA) trajectories two years after TKA are unclear. This study examined PA levels from baseline to two years post-TKA, quantified return to baseline PA levels over time, and evaluated associations between baseline participant characteristics and post-TKA PA levels.
METHODS: This was an exploratory secondary analysis of a randomized controlled trial. Participants (n = 135) aged 50 to 85 years undergoing primary unilateral TKA wore accelerometers preoperatively and 10 weeks, six months, and two years post-TKA to characterize light PA, moderate-vigorous PA (MVPA), and steps/day. Descriptive statistics were used to characterize PA levels. Repeated measures models estimated PA levels over time. The percentage of participants who returned to or exceeded baseline PA levels over time was quantified. Multivariate logistic regressions modeled return to baseline PA levels over time to evaluate associations with baseline participant characteristics. All models controlled for age, sex, and treatment group.
RESULTS: There was an increase of 8% steps/day and 0.75% MVPA from baseline to two years post-TKA. At two years post-TKA, 54.2, 53.1, and 55.6% of participants returned to baseline light PA, MVPA, and steps/day levels. Higher baseline PA levels were associated with lower odds of returning to baseline levels at all timepoints for MVPA (10 weeks odds ratio (95% confidence interval): 0.62 (0.46 to 0.84); six months: 0.55 (0.40 to 0.76); two years: 0.52 (0.36 to 0.75)), as well as light PA and steps/day (all P-values < 0.05). Baseline body mass index, Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Arthritis Index scores, and Functional Comorbidity Index were associated inconsistently with PA levels.
CONCLUSION: While on average, PA levels increased from baseline to two years post-TKA, participants who have higher baseline PA levels had reduced odds of returning to the same level. These findings suggest TKA and current rehabilitation may not fully address PA, and additional support (e.g., behavioral guidance or tailored rehabilitation) may be needed.

title: Clinical and functional predictors of delayed return to sport after first-time patellar dislocation in adolescents: A prospective cohort study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: First-time lateral patellar dislocation is common in adolescent athletes and may cause persistent functional impairment despite nonoperative treatment. Early predictors of delayed return to sport remain incompletely defined.
OBJECTIVE: To identify early clinical and functional factors associated with delayed return to unrestricted preinjury-level sport after first-time lateral patellar dislocation in adolescents.
METHODS: This prospective cohort study included 160 adolescents aged 12-18 years (97 females, 63 males) with first-time traumatic lateral patellar dislocation managed nonoperatively. Participants underwent standardized rehabilitation and were followed for 12 months. At 3 months, quadriceps limb-symmetry index (LSI), single-leg hop performance, Y-Balance asymmetry, patellar apprehension, Banff Patellofemoral Instability Instrument 2.0 (BPII 2.0), and Pediatric International Knee Documentation Committee scores were assessed. Delayed return to sport was defined as failure to resume unrestricted preinjury-level sport within 6 months. Associations were evaluated using multivariable logistic regression.
RESULTS: Seventy-six participants (47.5%) experienced delayed return to sport. Compared with timely returners, they had lower quadriceps LSI, poorer hop performance, greater Y-Balance asymmetry, more frequent patellar apprehension, and worse patient-reported function. Independent predictors were each 10-percentage-point decrease in quadriceps LSI (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 1.82, 95% CI 1.29-2.57), persistent patellar apprehension (aOR 2.71, 95% CI 1.31-5.62), and each 10-point decrease in BPII 2.0 score (aOR 1.51, 95% CI 1.13-2.02). The model showed good discrimination (AUC 0.80, 95% CI 0.73-0.86).
CONCLUSION: Reduced quadriceps symmetry, persistent apprehension, and poorer instability-specific function were independently associated with delayed return to sport, supporting multidimensional, criterion-based rehabilitation in adolescents.

title: Preoperative factors associated with quadriceps strength 1 year after total knee arthroplasty: a prospective longitudinal study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Quadriceps strength is highly related to physical function following total knee arthroplasty (TKA). Preoperative factors associated with long-term postoperative strength remain insufficiently understood. The aim of this exploratory study was to investigate preoperative factors associated with normalized quadriceps strength (NQS), changes in NQS and limb symmetry index (LSI) 1 year after TKA in patients with uncomplicated recovery.
METHODS: A prospective longitudinal study was conducted. Measurements took place at three primary care rehabilitation facilities in Region Västra Götaland, Sweden. The final analysis included 39 participants aged 65 years or older who underwent elective fast-track primary TKA due to knee osteoarthritis and had an uncomplicated recovery. Preoperative factors associated with NQS in the operated limb after 1 year (n = 39), changes in NQS from preoperative testing to 1 year after TKA (n = 39), and LSI (n = 35) were analyzed in three separate exploratory multiple linear regression models. Preoperative factors included age, sex, NQS, the 6-minute walk test (6MWT), and the LSI.
RESULTS: Preoperative NQS (B = 0.72, 95% CI: 0.40 to 1.0, p < 0.001) and LSI (B = - 0.17, 95% CI: - 0.29 to - 0.037, p = 0.013) were significantly associated with NQS 1 year after TKA. LSI was the only preoperative factor significantly associated with changes in NQS (B = - 0.19, 95% CI: - 0.32 to - 0.059, p = 0.006) and LSI 1 year after TKA (B = 0.41, 95% CI: 0.15 to 0.68, p = 0.004).
CONCLUSIONS: In this selected and relatively small sample, greater normalized quadriceps strength in the operated limb and higher LSI 1 year after TKA appeared to be primarily associated with higher preoperative normalized quadriceps strength in the operated limb and higher preoperative LSI, respectively, whereas strength gains appeared to be associated with lower preoperative LSI. The findings should be considered exploratory and primarily applicable to older adults with uncomplicated recovery after TKA. Confirmation in larger studies is warranted.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: Retrospectively registered February 9, 2022 ( http://clinicaltrials.gov , ID: NCT05248815).

title: Effects of Yeast Protein-Whey Protein Composite Supplementation on Recovery from Exercise-Induced Muscle Damage in Well-Trained Athletes: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
abstract: Objectives: Exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD) can impair muscle function and subsequent athletic performance. This study examined whether an isonitrogenous yeast protein-whey protein composite (YP) modifies recovery from EIMD compared with whey protein (WP) and a water-only control (C) in well-trained athletes. Methods: In this prospective, randomized, three-arm trial, 54 athletes were allocated to YP, WP, or C; 48 completed all follow-up procedures. YP and WP provided 0.9 g·kg-1·day-1 of actual protein, whereas C received water only and was not energy or sensory matched to the protein interventions. After 7 days of supplementation, participants completed a bilateral isokinetic EIMD protocol; supplementation continued through the 48 h assessment. Outcomes were assessed before EIMD, immediately afterward, and at 24, 48, and 72 h and were organized into muscle damage and soreness, inflammatory responses, and muscle function and performance. Female and male athletes were analyzed separately using linear mixed-effects models with multiplicity-adjusted contrasts. The study was not powered to formally compare intervention effects between sexes. Results: EIMD produced time-dependent biochemical, perceptual, and functional changes. Holm-adjusted comparisons showed lower CK in YP than C at 24 h in females and 48 h in males. The female 24 h CK finding was considered exploratory because the corresponding group × time interaction did not remain significant after damage-domain BH-FDR correction; the immediate male YP-C difference was significant only in the log-scale analysis. In males, YP was associated with lower soreness averaged across assessments and a lower immediate post-EIMD IL-6 value than C. Selected male CMJ comparisons favored YP but were exploratory after broader multiplicity correction. Acute-decline analyses showed smaller losses with YP in bilateral MVC and right-leg eccentric peak torque in males; only the right-leg eccentric YP-C comparison remained significant after BH-FDR correction. Conclusions: Compared with water alone, YP favorably influenced selected biochemical, perceptual, and muscle-function responses following EIMD, with the clearest pattern observed in the male analysis. Its overall response pattern was broadly aligned with WP, supporting the recovery-related potential and practical value of incorporating yeast-derived protein into a whey-based formulation.

title: Comparison of short-foot and toe-curl exercises on movement control during single-leg landing after ACL reconstruction: An exploratory randomized controlled trial.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To compare the effects of short-foot exercise (SFE) and toe-curl exercise (TCE) on movement control during single-leg landing in individuals undergoing anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR).
DESIGN: Multicenter exploratory randomized controlled trial.
SETTING: One hospital and two outpatient orthopedic clinics.
PARTICIPANTS: Thirty-eight individuals who had undergone ACLR and demonstrated dynamic knee valgus during a single-leg landing task.
MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES: Participants were randomized to the SFE or TCE group, performed the allocated exercises daily, and received supervised exercise therapy once weekly for 12 weeks. The primary outcome was hip adduction excursion during single-leg landing. Assessments were conducted at baseline, 6 weeks, and 12 weeks and analyzed using mixed models for repeated measures.
RESULTS: At 6 weeks, hip adduction excursion was lower in the SFE group than in the TCE group, with a between-group difference of -6.30° (95% confidence interval [CI], -9.19 to -3.41; effect size [ES], -1.41). The between-group difference in change from baseline was -6.98° (95% CI, -9.88 to -4.08; ES, -1.57). At 12 weeks, hip adduction excursion remained lower in the SFE group.
CONCLUSIONS: SFE may facilitate earlier improvement in frontal-plane movement control in patients who have undergone ACLR.

title: Shear wave elastography for assessing lower extremity muscle stiffness after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction: A systematic review.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) restores passive joint stability, yet athletes who meet strength benchmarks may still land stiffly, hesitate to push off, and re-injure. Muscle stiffness governs how rapidly force is transmitted to the joint, and shear wave elastography (SWE) quantifies it muscle by muscle, but SWE findings after ACLR have not been synthesized.
METHODS: Scopus, PubMed, SPORTDiscus, and CINAHL were searched through November 2025 following PRISMA 2020. Eligible studies compared SWE-derived lower-extremity muscle stiffness after ACLR with contralateral limbs or controls. Two reviewers independently screened, extracted data, and appraised quality (Downs and Black). Findings were synthesized narratively with Hedges' g (95% confidence intervals) where data permitted.
FINDINGS: Six studies (173 ACLR participants, 79 controls; quality poor to good) were included. Reduced passive vastus medialis shear modulus was consistently observed in operative limbs (g - 1.10 to -1.21 versus controls) and was associated with quadriceps strength, knee function, and landing biomechanics. Semitendinosus stiffness was reduced after hamstring tendon harvest (g - 1.29 to -1.64) but not at mid-belly after return to sport. Longitudinal deficits persisted at three months; active-contraction findings conflicted. No study sampled the distal vastus medialis obliquus or the distal hamstring musculotendinous region.
INTERPRETATION: SWE detects muscle-specific mechanical deficits that relate to function beyond strength: a compliant vastus medialis offers a mechanical explanation for the strong patient who lands stiffly, and reduced semitendinosus stiffness marks donor-site morbidity. Standardized protocols that sample clinically relevant regions and follow patients to return to sport are needed before SWE can guide rehabilitation.

title: Efficacy and safety study of diclofenac epolamine topical patch in accelerating rehabilitation of moderate hamstring strain: A randomized controlled trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Moderate hamstring strain is a common sports injury impairing daily and athletic function. While topical nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) offer localized pain relief with reduced systemic effects, high-quality evidence specific to hamstring injury is limited.
OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the effect of a short-course topical diclofenac epolamine patch combined with rehabilitation on pain and functional recovery in moderate hamstring strain.
METHODS: In this single-center, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 120 patients were randomized to an experimental group (diclofenac patch twice daily for 14 days plus rehabilitation) or a control group (placebo patch plus identical rehabilitation). Outcomes assessed included pain measured by the Visual Analogue Scale (VAS), as the primary endpoint, muscle strength, knee range of motion (ROM), functional back-kick test, time to rehabilitation criteria and safety (adverse events, liver/renal function).
RESULTS: The diclofenac group demonstrated significantly greater pain reduction at days 14, 21 and 28 post-intervention (all p < 0.01). Muscle strength recovery was superior at days 21 and 28, knee ROM improved more at day 28 and functional back-kick performance was better at day 28 (all p < 0.05). Time to meet rehabilitation criteria was significantly shorter in the experimental group (p = 0.002). Adverse event incidence and changes in liver/renal function were similar between groups (all p > 0.05).
CONCLUSION: A short-course topical diclofenac epolamine patch, combined with rehabilitation training, effectively alleviates pain, accelerates functional recovery, and is safe for treating moderate hamstring strain, supporting its use in clinical and sports rehabilitation.

title: Effect of tangeretin supplements on simulated precompetition weight loss in female combat sports athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Weight reduction before competition has long been a major challenge for combat-sports athletes. Unscientific weight-loss practices not only increase the risk of hormonal imbalance, electrolyte disturbance, and impaired immune function but also compromise athletic capacities such as aerobic and anaerobic performance and explosive power. This study investigated the potential benefits of tangeretin, a natural citrus extract, on athletic performance. These benefits include the regulation of hormone secretion, the optimization of carbohydrate and lipid metabolism, and the promotion of muscle synthesis and lipid utilization, which may help athletes reach their target weight.
OBJECTIVE: To examine the effects of tangeretin supplementation on body-composition and sports-performance indicators in female combat-sports athletes, and to evaluate its efficacy for simulated precompetition weight loss.
METHODS: Thirty female combat-sports athletes (4 wrestlers, 3 boxers, 9 sanda athletes, 3 judokas, and 11 taekwondo athletes) were recruited. A paired, randomized, double-blind design was used. All 30 participants were first paired according to sport and competitive level, then randomly allocated to either a tangeretin group or a placebo group (15 per group). The 30-day intervention comprised a double-blind nutritional supplement, a dietary questionnaire, blood sampling and analysis, body-composition assessment, isokinetic muscle-strength testing, and aerobic-capacity testing, to evaluate the effects of tangeretin (400 mg/day) on performance and health-related outcomes. These outcomes included body-composition indicators (e.g. body-fat percentage, fat mass, lean-body mass), fat-distribution indicators (e.g. limb and regional fat mass, gynoid fat mass), glucose and lipid-metabolism indicators (e.g. LDL-C, total cholesterol, free fatty acids), hormone indicators (e.g. cortisol, testosterone), muscle-strength indicators (e.g. peak torque of hip, knee, and ankle flexors and extensors), and maximal-oxygen-uptake-derived indicators (e.g. VO2max heart rate, time to exhaustion). Statistical significance was assessed using two-way repeated-measures analysis of variance (ANOVA).
RESULTS: (1) Body weight: 80.0% of athletes in the tangeretin group lost weight to varying degrees, and 33.3% (5 athletes) reached their competition weight class. (2) Body fat: body-fat percentage in the tangeretin group decreased from 23.92 ± 0.87% to 22.92 ± 0.89%; trunk, upper-limb, lower-limb, and android-region fat mass decreased by 6.77%, 8.77%, 4.43%, and 8.09%, respectively. (3) Glucose and lipid metabolism: HDL-C increased by 8.86% (P = 0.002), whereas triglycerides decreased by 25.00% (P = 0.048). (4) Sports performance: peak torque during hip, knee, and ankle flexion and extension increased significantly in the tangeretin group. VO2max also improved from 42.80 ± 1.13 to 43.46 ± 1.32 ml/kg/min.
CONCLUSION: Tangeretin supplementation effectively reduced body weight and fat mass (both overall and regionally) in female combat-sports athletes. Among the participants, 80.0% lost weight to varying degrees, and 33.3% reached their competition weight class, indicating a strong effect on precompetition weight loss. Moreover, tangeretin improved aerobic capacity and lower-limb joint muscle strength, thereby enhancing competitive performance.

title: Comparative efficacy of ultrasound-guided intra-articular injection of platelet-rich plasma (PRP), hydrolyzed type I collagen, and hyaluronic acid in patients with knee osteoarthritis: a randomized controlled trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Intra-articular therapies are widely used for knee osteoarthritis (KOA), but direct comparisons between emerging biomaterials such as hydrolyzed collagen (HC) and established options like platelet-rich plasma (PRP) and hyaluronic acid (HA) are limited.
OBJECTIVE: To compare the efficacy of intra-articular PRP, HC, and HA on pain, stiffness, and functional outcomes in KOA.
METHODS: In this randomized, assessor- and statistician-blinded trial, 135 patients with Kellgren-Lawrence grade 2-3 KOA were assigned (1:1:1) to receive three ultrasound-guided Intra-articular injections of PRP, HC, or HA at two-week intervals. The primary outcome was change in WOMAC total score at 6 months. Secondary outcomes included WOMAC subscales, VAS pain, and the Lequesne Index.
RESULTS: One hundred twenty-six patients completed follow-up. All groups showed significant improvements (p < 0.001). HA demonstrated greater improvements in some outcome measures at 1 month. PRP and HC demonstrated more sustained improvements than HA during 1 to 6 months follow-ups, although statistically significant between-group differences were limited to selected outcomes. No serious adverse events occurred.
CONCLUSION: Intra-articular PRP, HC, and HA improved outcomes in mild to moderate knee OA; PRP and HC showed a trend toward more sustained benefits during 1 to 6 months. Longer-term trials are necessary to confirm these findings.

title: Exercise, Medicine and Icing (EMI) for the Knee: Small Instalments, Big Gains in Early Osteoarthritis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Early knee osteoarthritis (OA) is a common cause of pain and functional limitation, often managed conservatively with medications and physiotherapy. The EMI protocol (Exercise, Medicine, and Icing) was developed as a surgeon-led, home-based intervention aimed at improving pain, function, and muscle strength in patients with early knee OA.
METHODS: This prospective, parallel-group, randomised controlled trial included 150 patients aged 40-70 years with Kellgren-Lawrence Grade 1-2 knee OA. Participants were randomised to receive either the EMI protocol (exercise, icing, and a standardised 6 week medical regimen including vitamin D, calcium, and magnesium supplementation) or the same medical regimen alone. The primary outcome was change in Visual Analog Scale (VAS) pain score at 6 weeks. Secondary outcomes included Kujala score, quadriceps strength (manual muscle testing), rescue NSAID use, adherence, and adverse events over 1 year.
RESULTS: At 1 year follow-up, 138 patients (92%) completed the study. The EMI group demonstrated significantly greater pain reduction (VAS 6.6 ± 1.1-1.9 ± 0.9) compared with Medicine Alone (6.5 ± 1.2-3.4 ± 1.2; p < 0.001). Functional outcomes (Kujala score), quadriceps strength, and reduction in rescue NSAID use were also significantly superior in the EMI group. Adherence to exercise and icing was high, and adverse events were minimal and comparable between groups.
CONCLUSION: The EMI protocol was associated with significantly greater improvements in pain, function, and quadriceps strength compared with medical therapy alone in patients with early knee OA. The findings support the incorporation of structured home-based exercise and cryotherapy into conservative management strategies for early knee OA.

title: Clinical and functional outcomes of aquatic plyometrics in adolescent patellofemoral pain syndrome: a dual-arm randomized controlled trial.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Optimal management of adolescent patellofemoral pain syndrome requires evidence-based interventions that maximize physical recovery without overloading the patellofemoral joint. This study investigated the efficacy of aquatic plyometric (Aquatic-Plyo) exercises on pain, muscle strength, and functional disability and health-related quality of life in this demographic.
DESIGN: A dual-arm randomized controlled trial.
SUBJECTS/PATIENTS: 56 adolescents with patellofemoral pain syndrome (age: 10-18 years).
METHODS: Adolescents were allocated to an experimental Aquatic-Plyo group or a control group performing conventional exercises. Both arms completed 45-min sessions twice weekly for 12 weeks. Pre- and post-treatment assessments included pain intensity, isokinetic knee (quadriceps and hamstrings) torque at 120°/s and 180°/s, functional disability, and health-related quality of life.
RESULTS: Mixed-model ANOVA confirmed the therapeutic dominance of the Aquatic-Plyo protocol. It yielded superior pain relief (p = 0.004, η2p = 0.14) and larger increases in quadriceps [120°/s (p = 0.006, η2p = 0.13); 180°/s (p = 0.008, η2p = 0.12)] and hamstring [120°/s (p = 0.007, η2p = 0.13); 180°/s (p = 0.023, η2p = 0.09)] peak torque. Moreover, the Aquatic-Plyo intervention drove greater reduction in functional disability (p = 0.03, η2p = 0.08) and notable enhancement in perceived health-related quality of life (p = 0.023, η2p = 0.09).
CONCLUSION: Aquatic-Plyo exercises effectively reduces pain and disability while improving muscle strength and health-related quality of life in adolescents with patellofemoral pain syndrome, making it a valuable addition to conservative rehabilitation strategies.

title: Platelet-Rich Plasma for Knee Osteoarthritis and Patient-Reported Outcomes: A Large Retrospective Analysis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) is used increasingly to treat knee osteoarthritis (OA). This study aimed to describe PRP use for knee OA and identify patient- and treatment-specific factors associated with clinical outcomes.
HYPOTHESIS: Patients with knee OA undergoing intra-articular PRP injections would demonstrate improvement in pain, function, and symptoms over time, with outcomes varying by patient and treatment characteristics.
STUDY DESIGN: Retrospective cohort study.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 3.
METHODS: A total of 743 patients with knee OA were treated with intra-articular PRP injections. Outcomes were assessed using the Numeric Rating Scale (NRS, 0-100, higher scores indicating greater pain) and the Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score for Joint Replacement (KOOS-JR). Change in patient-reported outcome measure (PROM) scores from baseline and achievement of patient acceptable symptom state (PASS) were measured. Repeated-measures mixed models evaluated outcomes at baseline, 6 months, and 1 year using an all-response analysis (391 patients for Pain NRS; 400 for KOOS-JR).
RESULTS: PRP injections were associated with improvement in pain, function, and symptom state. Pain NRS improved from 39.2 at baseline to 27.2 at 6 months and 22.4 at 1 year (both P < 0.001), while KOOS-JR improved from 60.7 to 68.5 and 69.1 (both P < 0.001), with similar findings in the complete-case cohort. When stratified by radiographic severity, patients with Kellgren-Lawrence (KL) grades 1 to 3 improved in both outcomes at 6 months and 1 year, while patients with KL grade 4 improved in Pain NRS at 1 year (P < 0.001) and KOOS-JR at 6 months (P = 0.01) and 1 year (P = 0.001). PASS achievement rates increased over time for both pain and function.
CONCLUSION: Intra-articular PRP injections were associated with improvements in pain, function, and symptoms in patients with knee OA. Differences between complete-case and all-response analyses suggest that follow-up patterns may influence estimated treatment response.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings describe patient-reported outcomes after intra-articular PRP injection for knee OA. Because this study lacked a control group, findings should not be interpreted as evidence that PRP caused the observed improvements.

title: Non-Surgical Therapies for Knee Osteoarthritis: Current Evidence and Emerging Strategies.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Knee osteoarthritis (OA) is a degenerative joint disease characterized by pain, stiffness, and functional impairment. As many patients seek to avoid surgery, a synthesis of conservative treatment options is clinically relevant for evidence-based management.
METHODS: A structured PubMed literature search was conducted through December 15, 2025. Eligible studies included randomized controlled trials, cohort and case-control studies, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses evaluating nonsurgical interventions for knee OA. Extracted outcomes included pain, function, safety, and comparative effectiveness across reported follow-up durations.
RESULTS: Intra-articular hyaluronic acid (HA) has a favorable safety profile and may delay progression to total knee arthroplasty, though benefits over placebo are modest and guideline recommendations inconsistent. Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) improves pain and function and may outperform HA, although outcomes vary with preparation methods and study quality. Autologous conditioned serum and dextrose prolotherapy demonstrate symptomatic benefit, whereas corticosteroid injections primarily provide short-term relief. Disease-modifying osteoarthritis drugs (DMOADs), including sprifermin, lorecivivint, LNA043, cathepsin-K inhibition, ADAMTS-5 inhibition, and repurposed metabolic agents such as metformin, are emerging investigational strategies with variable structural and symptomatic results. Early evidence suggests mesenchymal stem cell-based therapies may improve outcomes but remain investigational. Core conservative measures, including exercise therapy, physical therapy, and weight reduction, consistently reduce pain and improve function. Assistive devices and valgus bracing provide additional symptomatic and biomechanical benefit. Among device-based interventions, cooled radiofrequency ablation offers durable pain relief compared with HA or corticosteroids, while sustained acoustic medicine and extracorporeal shockwave therapy show functional improvement; evidence for pulsed electromagnetic field therapy is mixed. Topical nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs provide effective analgesia with reduced systemic risk.
CONCLUSION: Non-surgical management of knee OA should follow a stepwise approach, with rehabilitation and weight optimization as first-line therapy, selective injection- and device-based options for persistent symptoms, and timely surgical referral when disability remains refractory. Future progress will depend on standardized protocols and higher-quality long-term comparative trials to improve treatment selection and disease modification.

title: Conservative Management of a Displaced Iliopsoas Avulsion in an Adolescent: A Case Report and Systematic Review.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To report a case of traumatic iliopsoas tendon avulsion with displacement exceeding the commonly cited 2-cm surgical threshold, managed successfully without surgery, and to systematically review the literature on optimal treatment and return-to-sport outcomes.
DESIGN: Case report combined with a PRISMA-compliant systematic review of PubMed, Cochrane Library, and Embase.
SETTING: Level I university trauma center; systematic review of published case reports and series.
PARTICIPANTS: A 16-year-old male competitive soccer player (index case) and 58 additional patients from the literature, predominantly adolescent males with sports-related iliopsoas avulsion.
INTERVENTIONS: The index patient received conservative treatment with staged weight bearing and structured physiotherapy. Across the literature, 90% (52/58) were treated conservatively and 10% operatively.
MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES: Clinical recovery, strength restoration, radiographic union on MRI, and return to sport.
RESULTS: Eighteen studies (58 patients; 59 including this case) were analyzed. A bony lesser-trochanter avulsion was present in 98% (57/58). Of at least 9 patients with displacement >2 cm, 5 recovered fully nonoperatively. The index patient was pain-free with full strength and unrestricted soccer return at 3 months; 6-month MRI showed radiographic nonunion despite complete functional recovery. Return to sport approached 100%, typically within 10 to 12 weeks.
CONCLUSIONS: Available very low-certainty evidence suggests that nonoperative management can achieve favorable clinical recovery and return to sport after traumatic iliopsoas avulsion, including in some cases with displacement greater than 2 cm. Return-to-sport decisions may reasonably prioritize restored, pain-free function over radiographic union, but larger prospective studies are needed.

title: Efficacy of combined therapies on degenerative joint disease of the temporomandibular joint: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the efficacy of intra-articular orthobiologics versus standard active control (arthrocentesis or hyaluronic acid) on pain, mouth opening and structural bone gain in advanced degenerative temporomandibular joint (TMJ) disease, stratified by orthobiologic class and joint compartment.
DESIGN: Systematic review with exploratory meta-analysis, following PRISMA and prospectively registered on PROSPERO (CRD420261425634), of RCTs published January 2020-June 2026. Outcomes were pooled as mean difference (MD) by orthobiologic class, with joint compartment as a three-level moderator. Clinical relevance was assessed against minimal important difference (MCID) thresholds; non-randomised studies were synthesised narratively.
RESULTS: Twenty-eight studies were included: 18 RCTs (≈862 patients; 12 pooled) and 10 narrative studies. Versus hyaluronic acid, orthobiologics reduced pain (MD -0.71) and improved mouth opening (MD 3.04 mm), both below the MCID. Versus arthrocentesis alone, effects were larger: pain (MD -1.57, exceeding the MCID) and mouth opening (MD 3.46 mm, below the MCID), with high heterogeneity unexplained by orthobiologic class. No RCT tested the dual joint space approach, represented only by one narrative study. A subset of studies had incomplete degenerative anchoring or unreported compartment. Certainty of evidence was low to very low.
CONCLUSIONS: Current evidence does not support a firm recommendation for any single orthobiologic in advanced degenerative TMJ disease, reinforcing a conservative, stepwise approach. Dual joint space therapy - a plausible but untested hypothesis - remains unstudied and is a priority for future research.

title: Effects of acute Capsaicin analogue intake on athletic performance: a three-level meta-analysis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Capsaicin analogues have been proposed as potential ergogenic aids, but their acute effects on athletic performance remain inconsistent. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of acute capsaicin analogue intake on exercise performance using a three-level meta-analysis.
METHODS: PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, SPORTDiscus, and the Cochrane Library were searched up to April 1, 2025. Randomized controlled trials examining acute oral capsaicin analogue intake in healthy adults were included. Outcomes were classified into strength, power, muscular endurance, and aerobic capacity. Hedges' g was calculated using a three-level random-effects model.
RESULTS: Twenty-one randomized crossover trials with 67 effect sizes were included. Acute capsaicin analogue intake significantly improved overall athletic performance compared with placebo (g = 0.20, 95% CI [0.07, 0.33], p < 0.01). Subgroup analyses showed significant effects on power (g = 0.39) and muscular endurance (g = 0.25), but not on strength or aerobic capacity. Phenylcapsaicin showed the largest effect, and benefits were more evident in trained participants. Dose-response analysis suggested a nonlinear pattern, with low-to-moderate doses showing more stable benefits.
CONCLUSIONS: Acute capsaicin analogue intake may produce small but significant improvements in athletic performance, particularly in power and muscular endurance. However, due to heterogeneity, publication bias, and very low certainty of evidence, these findings should be interpreted cautiously.

title: Isometric Strength, Joint Mobility, and Muscle Strength Ratios Among Female Artistic Swimmers from the Spanish National Artistic Swimming Team: A Cross-Sectional Study Across Age Categories.
abstract: Background and Objectives: Artistic swimming demands high levels of strength, joint mobility, and body control; however, the physical profiles of elite athletes in this sport remain insufficiently characterized. This study aimed to characterize and compare isometric strength, joint mobility, inter-limb differences, and muscle strength ratios across the Youth, Junior, and Senior age categories of the Spanish National Artistic Swimming Team. Methods: This cross-sectional observational study included 36 elite female artistic swimmers, defined by their selection for the Spanish National Artistic Swimming Team: 11 Youth, 12 Junior, and 13 Senior athletes. Anthropometric characteristics, shoulder and hip ranges of motion assessed using photographic goniometry, upper- and lower-limb isometric strength, handgrip strength, and countermovement jump height were evaluated. Age categories were compared using the Kruskal-Wallis test, followed by Dunn's post hoc comparisons with Holm correction. Inter-limb differences were analyzed using the Wilcoxon test. Results: Senior athletes generally exhibited greater isometric strength than younger age categories. Among the main between-category differences, Senior athletes showed greater normalized shoulder internal-rotation strength than Youth athletes (1.56 vs. 0.95 N/kg; group-specific 95% CIs around the means: 1.43-1.69 and 0.80-1.11, respectively) and greater hip-abduction strength (2.34 vs. 1.71 N/kg; group-specific 95% CIs around the means: 2.07-2.60 and 1.51-1.93, respectively). The corresponding omnibus Kruskal-Wallis effect sizes were η2 = 0.40 and η2 = 0.32, respectively. Differences were observed in CMJ height and absolute right handgrip strength. No significant differences were observed after normalizing handgrip strength to body mass. Between-category differences were observed in certain measures of hip mobility but not in shoulder mobility. Inter-limb differences were limited to specific variables. Conclusions: These findings provide a preliminary descriptive characterization of elite female artistic swimmers and reveal differences between age categories, primarily in specific strength variables. These cross-sectional differences between age categories should not be interpreted as evidence of developmental adaptations or training-induced changes. Given the cross-sectional design and small group sizes, the application of these findings to athlete monitoring, training, or the interpretation of inter-limb differences requires confirmation in longitudinal studies.

title: Pre-sleep milk-derived proteins do not impair sleep or recovery in elite female athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Sleep is essential for athlete recovery and performance, yet athletes frequently experience restricted or poor-quality sleep. Pre-sleep feeding (PSF) has emerged as a strategy to support recovery, but randomized, double-blinded, crossover trials comparing PSF macronutrient options on objective and subjective sleep outcomes in elite female athletes remain limited.
METHODS: Twenty-five National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) Division I female athletes (18-25 years old) were recruited; 21 completed the trial. In a randomized, double-blinded, placebo controlled, crossover design conducted over 4-8 weeks, participants consumed four treatments for three consecutive nights each: 40 g casein protein (CAS; 160 kcal), 40 g α-lactalbumin protein (ALA; 160 kcal), 40 g carbohydrate (CHO; 160 kcal), and 40g of a placebo (PLA; 5 kcal), with a minimum three-day washout between conditions. Supplements were consumed ~2 h after the final meal and ~30 min before bedtime as the last caloric intake of the day. Objective outcomes were obtained from the WHOOP 4.0 device (total sleep time (TST), sleep onset latency (SOL), sleep efficiency (SE), resting heart rate (RHR), and heart rate variability (HRV)). Subjective outcomes were assessed each morning via questionnaires (subjective sleep quality (SSQ), subjective sleep onset latency (SSOL), and subjective recovery (SREC)). Nocturnal interstitial glucose was assessed via blinded continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) in a subset (n = 6). Sleep and recovery variables were analyzed using one-way repeated-measures analysis of variance (ANOVA) to evaluate treatment effects across the four supplementation conditions. For CGM data, a two-way repeated-measures ANOVA was used to evaluate main effects of treatment and time, as well as the treatment × time interaction. Tukey's post hoc testing was used with significance set at p < 0.05.
RESULTS: No significant treatment effects were observed for TST, SOL, SE, RHR, or HRV (p > 0.05). TST ranged from 7.47-7.62 h, SE from 91.5-92.0%, RHR from 53.5-54.1 bpm, and HRV from 98.2-103.9 ms across conditions. No significant treatment effects were detected for SSQ, SSOL, or SREC (p > 0.05); SSQ ranged from 69-75%, SSOL from 16-20 min, and SREC from 61-66%. In the CGM sub-analysis, a main effect of time was observed for nocturnal glucose (p = 0.008), but no differences among treatments (p = 0.187) or a time × treatment interaction (p = 0.550) were detected.
CONCLUSIONS: In NCAA Division I female athletes, three consecutive nights of pre-sleep ingestion of CAS, ALA, or CHO did not impair objective or subjective measures of sleep or recovery compared with PLA. These findings demonstrate that pre-sleep feeding, regardless of macronutrient type, can be incorporated without negatively affecting sleep quality or recovery metrics.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov (Identifier: STUDY00004409).

title: Cold-Water Immersion for Post-exercise Recovery: An Overlap-Aware Umbrella Review.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cold-water immersion (CWI) is widely used after strenuous exercise, but review-level findings vary by outcome, comparator, recovery window, population, and protocol. Reuse of the same primary studies across reviews can also exaggerate apparent consistency.
METHODS: We searched PubMed, Web of Science, SPORTDiscus, Cochrane Library, Embase, and Scopus from inception to 30 January 2026 for systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and network meta-analyses of post-exercise CWI. Fourteen reviews were included. Primary-study overlap was quantified using the corrected covered area (CCA) overall and for outcome-specific study-to-review mappings. Because overlap was high and review-level estimates were statistically dependent, we did not perform second-order meta-analysis. Source-verified estimates were synthesized in a structured, overlap-aware format. Methodological quality was assessed with AMSTAR 2.
RESULTS: Of the 14 included reviews, 13 provided quantitative estimates, whereas one review provided narrative evidence on heart rate variability (HRV). Overall CCA was 12.68% (high); 99 of 165 primary-study families appeared in at least two reviews. Outcome-specific CCA was 15.03% for delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS; very high) and ranged from 0.00% for interleukin-6 (IL-6) to 25.00% for C-reactive protein (CRP). It was not calculable for HRV, because one review contributed. AMSTAR 2 confidence was low in 2 reviews and critically low in 12. DOMS showed the most consistent favorable pattern: source-review standardized mean differences ranged from -1.04 to -0.37, although the largest estimate was soccer-specific and its 95% prediction interval crossed zero. Because DOMS evidence was highly redundant across the contributing reviews, this apparent consistency does not represent independent replications. Findings for objective performance and biochemical outcomes were inconsistent, time-dependent, or comparator-dependent.
CONCLUSIONS: Within the available review-level evidence, CWI was associated with the most consistent reduction in self-reported short-term post-exercise DOMS, but the clinical importance of the observed effects remains uncertain. Evidence does not support a uniform benefit across objective performance or inflammatory outcomes. Protocol observations, including commonly studied temperatures and durations, are descriptive and should not be interpreted as an optimized prescription. Trial Registration PROSPERO CRD420261332482.

title: Smartphone-derived mobility metrics identify distinct recovery phenotypes following ACL reconstruction: associations with function, pain, and psychological health.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Recovery after anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction is typically monitored through patient-reported outcomes and periodic clinical assessments, which may not fully capture real-world functional performance. Smartphone-derived mobility data provide a passive and objective approach for evaluating daily activity and recovery.
PURPOSE: To examine associations between smartphone-derived mobility metrics and recovery outcomes in adults 3-12 months after primary ACL reconstruction and to identify distinct recovery phenotypes using mobility-based clustering.
METHODS: This cross-sectional study included 120 adults who were 3-12 months post-primary ACL reconstruction and had at least 14 days of retrospective smartphone mobility data. Mobility variables included daily step count, activity volume and intensity (e.g., active minutes and walking bout duration), sedentary behavior, and walking-related metrics. Outcomes included pain (Numeric Rating Scale [NRS]), functional status (Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score [KOOS] Pain, Activities of Daily Living, and Sport/Recreation subscales), knee-related quality of life (ACL Quality of Life questionnaire [ACL-QoL]), and psychological measures including the Pain Catastrophizing Scale (PCS), Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9), and Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7). Associations were evaluated using Pearson correlation and multivariable linear regression analyses. Recovery phenotypes were identified using unsupervised k-means clustering of mobility metrics.
RESULTS: Higher daily step counts were independently associated with better KOOS-ADL scores (β = 0.48, p < 0.001), higher ACL-QoL scores (β = 0.45, p < 0.001), and lower pain intensity (β = - 0.39, p = 0.001). Three recovery phenotypes emerged: a high-activity/low-pain phenotype with superior function and minimal psychological distress, a moderate-activity/moderate-pain phenotype with intermediate outcomes, and a low-activity/high-pain phenotype characterized by reduced mobility, poorer function, greater pain, and higher pain catastrophizing. Significant gradients were observed across phenotypes for pain (NRS: 1.72-5.01), function (KOOS-Pain: 88.94-62.37), and pain catastrophizing (PCS: 8.52-24.91; all p < 0.001).
CONCLUSIONS: Smartphone-derived mobility metrics were significantly associated with recovery outcomes following ACL reconstruction. Mobility-based clustering identified distinct recovery phenotypes associated with meaningful differences in pain, function, and pain catastrophizing, highlighting the potential of passive mobility monitoring to support personalized rehabilitation strategies. However, given the variability in evaluation periods and uncontrolled surgical factors, future research employing standardized, long-term follow-ups is warranted.

title: Reliability and validity of the My Jump Lab app for assessing vertical jump performance after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: To evaluate the test-retest reliability and validity of My Jump Lab compared with a force platform for assessing vertical jump performance after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR).
METHODS: A total of 102 individuals, 6-24 months post-ACLR and cleared for return-to-sport (RTS) testing, performed the single-leg vertical jump (SLVJ) and single-leg drop jump (SLDJ), assessed using My Jump Lab and a force platform. Jump height derived from flight time (FT) and take-off velocity (ToV), reactive strength index (RSI) and limb symmetry index (LSI) were analyzed. Test-retest reliability, inter-instrument reliability, agreement and association, diagnostic accuracy, and association with force-platform-derived kinetic (force at zero velocity, peak landing force, and concentric net impulse) variables were assessed.
RESULTS: My Jump Lab demonstrated excellent test-retest reliability (intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) = 0.992-0.997; standard error of measurement = 0.24-0.41 cm; minimal detectable change = 0.65-1.14 cm). Associations with the force platform were strong to very strong for jump height (r = 0.786-0.987), RSI (r = 0.975), and LSI (r = 0.760-0.983). Inter-instrument reliability was excellent for FT and RSI (ICC = 0.974-0.983) and fair for ToV (ICC = 0.750). Bland-Altman analyses showed mean biases ranging from -1.21 to -0.08 cm for jump height and -0.29 cm/s for RSI. Accuracy for LSI ≥ 90% ranged from 87.3% to 94.1%. SLVJ jump height showed moderate-to-good associations with force-platform-derived kinetic (r = 0.534-0.678).
CONCLUSIONS: My Jump Lab provides reliable and valid measures of vertical jump performance post-ACLR and may complement RTS assessment when force platforms are unavailable.

title: Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction and Mental Health: A Bidirectional Relationship.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: New-onset mental health (MH) conditions are a concern for patients undergoing anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction. Patients with pre-existing MH conditions have been observed to experience poorer postoperative outcomes.
HYPOTHESIS: Patients with pre-existing MH diagnoses would report poorer outcomes after ACL reconstruction, and non-sport-related injuries would be associated with a greater incidence of new MH diagnoses.
STUDY DESIGN: Retrospective cohort study.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 3.
METHODS: Adults undergoing ACL reconstruction between October 2016 and October 2023 at a large university-affiliated practice were included. Patients completed the Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS) Global Health and Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcomes Score (KOOS) before surgery, and at multiple postoperative timepoints. MH diagnoses included anxiety, depression, bipolar disorder, and other psychiatric conditions documented through medications, International Classification of Diseases, tenth revision codes or chart notes. Continuous and categorical variables were compared using appropriate univariate tests, and mixed-model linear regression was used to compare patient-reported outcomes over time while controlling for patient sex.
RESULTS: Out of 365 patients undergoing ACL reconstruction, 50 (13.7%) had a pre-existing MH diagnosis (mean age, 36.42; 84.0% female). Groups did not differ on any scale at baseline except PROMIS Mental Health, which was lower among patients with a pre-existing MH diagnosis (47.3 vs 53.6; P < 0.001). The MH Group reported significantly worse KOOS scores at 2 weeks postoperatively, but no differences were observed thereafter. Among 315 patients without previous history of MH disorder (mean age, 32.90; 52.7% female), 8 (2.5%) developed a new MH diagnosis at 1-year follow-up. Patients aged ≤25 years demonstrated significantly higher baseline KOOS scores than patients >25 years. Among 294 sport-related injuries and 71 non-sport-related injuries, non-sport-related injuries were associated with lower baseline KOOS and PROMIS scores, and higher incidence of new MH diagnoses (7% vs 1.6%; P = 0.02).
CONCLUSION: No differences in KOOS outcomes beyond 2 weeks were found between patients with and without a pre-existing MH condition. Furthermore, non-sport-related injuries were associated with a higher rate of new MH diagnoses.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings may help clinicians identify patients who could benefit from additional support during recovery.

title: Autologous Peripheral Blood-Derived Stem Cells Combined with Platelet-Rich Plasma is Associated With Clinical and Radiological Improvement in Anterior Cruciate Ligament Ruptures-Preliminary Clinical and MRI Findings in 47 Consecutive Patients.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) ruptures are common injuries in young and active individuals and can lead to long-term functional impairment and early onset osteoarthritis. While ACL reconstruction remains the standard of care, recent evidence suggests that spontaneous healing may be possible in selected cases. Regenerative and biologic treatment concepts have therefore gained increasing interest. This study investigates the clinical and radiological outcomes of a stem cell-based regenerative treatment for traumatic ACL ruptures and presents findings as preliminary observational evidence.
METHODS: In this single-center retrospective case series, 47 patients with isolated partial and complete traumatic anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) ruptures were treated using a biologic, non-surgical protocol. Diagnosis of an ACL rupture was confirmed by standardized clinical examination (Lachman test, anterior drawer test, and pivot shift test) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), which was additionally used to assess rupture morphology and synovial sheath integrity. All patients underwent an ultrasound-guided injection of autologous biologic products derived from peripheral venous blood, consisting of 8 mL of an autologous blood-derived stem cell preparation (BSC), comprising approximately 2-3 mL of concentrated mononuclear cells suspended in 6 mL of autologous platelet-containing plasma, injected directly into the torn ACL. Patients were allowed immediate full weight-bearing without bracing and followed a standardized physiotherapy program. Clinical follow-up was conducted for 12 months, including assessment of pain (VAS), functional outcomes (IKDC, Lysholm), return-to-sport timelines, and MRI-based evaluation of ligament morphology.
RESULTS: The mean age of the cohort was 28.1 years (95% CI 26.0-30.2). Functional outcomes improved continuously throughout follow-up, with mean IKDC and Lysholm scores of 93.6 (95% CI 92.4-94.8) and 94.0 (95% CI 92.7-95.3), respectively, at 12 months. Pain levels decreased markedly, reaching a mean VAS score of 0.36 (95% CI 0.19-0.53). Patients returned to running after a mean of 2.19 weeks (95% CI 1.93-2.45), and most resumed their pre-injury activity level by one year. No infections or re-ruptures occurred and only one secondary ACL reconstruction was recorded. Patients with an intact synovial sheath demonstrated faster return to pivoting sports (26.8 vs. 33.2 weeks) compared with patients with a complete ACL rupture. MRI at 3 months showed evidence of improved ligament morphology in all but one patient.
CONCLUSIONS: This preliminary case series suggests that stem cell-based biologic stimulation may be associated with functional recovery and radiological improvement in selected patients with ACL ruptures. Prospective controlled trials are required to validate these findings.

title: Effects of Oral L-Arginine on Everyday Persistent Fatigue, Sleep, and Post-Exercise Lactate Recovery in Community-Dwelling Working-Age Adults: A Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Randomized Trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: The evidence for nutritional interventions against fatigue is limited; we evaluated whether L-arginine reduces fatigue in working-age adults.
METHODS: In this 8-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 120 community-dwelling working-age adults aged 30-59 years with persistent fatigue (Fatigue Severity Scale [FSS] total ≥ 27) received oral L-arginine 3 g/day, 6 g/day, or placebo. The primary endpoint was FSS change; secondary endpoints included the Checklist Individual Strength (CIS), Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), and blood lactate kinetics during a standardized submaximal treadmill run (~70% VO2max, 30 min). Data from 119 participants were analyzed, with Holm adjustment for multiplicity.
RESULTS: At Week 8, FSS decreased more with 6 g/day than with placebo (-6.41 vs. -2.23; Holm-adjusted p = 0.024), whereas 3 g/day did not differ from placebo. The 6 g/day CIS improvement did not survive multiplicity adjustment. PSQI scores improved nominally at both doses (3 g/day, p = 0.007; 6 g/day, p = 0.045). With 6 g/day, the total lactate area under the curve (Holm-adjusted p = 0.041) and 15-min recovery lactate (Holm-adjusted p = 0.002) were lower than with the placebo, whereas the resting plasma nitrite did not differ. No serious adverse events occurred.
CONCLUSIONS: L-arginine supplementation at 6 g/day for 8 weeks reduced fatigue severity relative to placebo and was well-tolerated; however, mean FSS scores remained above the enrollment threshold, indicating a reduction in, rather than resolution of, persistent fatigue.

title: Orthobiologics for hand and wrist disorders: An indication-specific systematic review and evidence-gap synthesis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Orthobiologics are increasingly used in hand and wrist disorders; however, their clinical effectiveness remains uncertain due to heterogeneity in indications, formulations, and outcome reporting.
METHODS: This systematic review was reported in accordance with PRISMA 2020 and prospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261359867). PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane CENTRAL, and Web of Science were searched from inception through March 31, 2026. Primary clinical studies evaluating locally delivered orthobiologics for hand or wrist disorders were eligible. Risk of bias was assessed using RoB 2 for randomized trials and ROBINS-I for nonrandomized comparative studies and the Joanna Briggs Institute checklist for uncontrolled case series; certainty was evaluated using GRADE. Because the studies differed substantially in indication, biologic formulation, comparator, follow-up, and outcome definition, meta-analysis was not clinically appropriate; a structured qualitative synthesis was performed.
RESULTS: Ten primary clinical studies were included: three studies of carpal tunnel syndrome, one of de Quervain tenosynovitis, three of trapeziometacarpal osteoarthritis, one of distal-radius fracture, and two of scaphoid nonunion. No meta-analysis was performed. Evidence for carpal tunnel syndrome was inconsistent across comparators and follow-up durations. In de Quervain tenosynovitis, PRP produced outcomes comparable to corticosteroid injection, with fewer reported local adverse effects. Evidence for trapeziometacarpal osteoarthritis was limited and comparator-dependent. In scaphoid nonunion, the primary BMP studies suggested possible osteoinductive benefit but also identified complications, including heterotopic ossification, persistent nonunion, and reoperation. Overall certainty ranged from moderate to very low.
CONCLUSIONS: Orthobiologic effectiveness for hand and wrist disorders appears indication-specific but is supported by limited and heterogeneous evidence. Routine PRP use in osteoarthritis is not supported, and application in other conditions should remain selective and context-dependent. Larger, adequately powered, placebo-controlled trials with standardized biologic characterization and outcome reporting are required. These findings should be interpreted as an evidence-gap map rather than proof of comparative efficacy.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV (systematic review of predominantly small randomized and nonrandomized studies with heterogeneous designs and limited sample sizes).

title: Quantitative UTE MRI Differences in the Meniscus Following ACL Reconstruction: A Prospective Cohort Study Using 3D Ultrashort Echo Time Adiabatic T1rho and Magnetization Transfer Imaging.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: ACLR is associated with altered joint loading and increased risk of post-traumatic osteoarthritis. Conventional MRI has limited sensitivity to early meniscal differences because of short-T2 signal decay and magic-angle effects.
PURPOSE: To evaluate whether 3D ultrashort echo time imaging-based adiabatic T1rho (UTE-Adiab-T1rho) and ultrashort echo time imaging-based macromolecular fraction (UTE-MMF) identify regional quantitative MRI differences after ACLR.
STUDY TYPE: Prospective longitudinal cohort study.
POPULATION: 30 control scans, 19 ACLR scans at 6-12 months, and 13 ACLR scans at 12+ months were analyzed. Mean ages were 34.5, 34.5, and 37.2 years; female/male counts were 15/15, 9/10, and 8/5.
FIELD STRENGTH/SEQUENCE: Participants underwent 3-T knee MRI with 3D fat-saturated UTE-Adiab-T1rho and UTE magnetization transfer sequences.
ASSESSMENT: UTE-Adiab-T1rho and UTE-MMF maps were generated with single-component exponential and two-pool magnetization transfer models. Values were extracted from four meniscal regions of interest by a blinded reader, with blinded redelineation in a subset. Patient-reported outcomes included International Knee Documentation Committee, Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score, and Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index scores.
STATISTICAL TESTS: Linear mixed-effects models accounted for repeated observations. Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction was applied.
RESULTS: UTE-Adiab-T1rho showed significant group (q = 0.001) and region (q < 0.001) effects. Compared with controls, UTE-Adiab-T1rho was higher in LAM at 6-12 months (+5.60 ms; q = 0.035) and 12+ months (+7.09 ms; q = 0.028), and in LPM at 12+ months (+6.35 ms; q = 0.035). UTE-MMF showed significant group (q = 0.041) and region (q < 0.001) effects. LPM UTE-MMF was lower than controls at 6-12 months (-3.56 percentage points; q = 0.028) and 12+ months (-3.10 percentage points; q = 0.049). No 6-12 versus 12+ month MRI or PROM contrast survived FDR correction. MRI-PROM associations were not FDR-significant (all q ≥ 0.383).
DATA CONCLUSION: UTE-Adiab-T1rho and UTE-MMF mapping identified regional MRI differences after ACLR. Pairwise differences were concentrated in lateral regions, but corrected group-by-region interactions were not significant. PROMs were worse after ACLR but did not differ between postoperative windows after correction.
EVIDENCE LEVEL: 2.
TECHNICAL EFFICACY STAGE: 2.

title: Characterising the Internal and External Load During Warm-Up, Match Play and Training in Soccer Substitutes: A Systematic Scoping Review.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Shorter match-play exposure for soccer substitutes relative to those who start matches has implications in the days before, during and following match play concerning their training, preparatory and recovery/compensatory practices. Specifically, characterising the internal and external loading of substitute players throughout a weekly microcycle can facilitate evidence-based recommendations aimed at optimising their performance readiness.
OBJECTIVES: This systematic scoping review aimed to map and characterise the internal and external loading associated with warm-up, match play and training in soccer substitutes.
METHODS: Prior to literature searches being conducted, a Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome, Study design (PICOS) statement was formed. Online database (PubMed, SPORTDiscus, Scopus and Web of Science) searches were performed according to PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) protocols. Studies were eligible if internal or external characteristics of soccer substitutes were measured in training or match-play scenarios. After calibration exercises, two authors independently quality assessed each study, with Cohen's kappa undertaken to assess inter-rater agreement. A scoping review methodology was selected because of the methodological and conceptual heterogeneity across studies, which precluded meaningful meta-analysis.
RESULTS: A total of 5135 studies were identified, 66 of which met study criteria. Substantive inter-rater agreement was observed (κ = 0.939, p < 0.001) during the quality assessment of included studies. Soccer substitutes' body temperature, and thus several aspects of physical performance, may not be maintained at time of pitch entry (body temperature pre-pitch entry ~ 37 °C vs match play > 38 °C). Substitutes may experience lower absolute physical loading during training and match day (e.g. match-day 'top up' activity: ~ 17 min; total distance: ~ 1700 m) but during match play, substitutes typically cover higher relative total distances (~ 109 to ~ 137 m·min-1), high-speed running (~ 9.8 to ~ 13.5 m·min-1) and sprinting distance (~ 3.8 to 5.0 m·min-1) compared with players who started the match. Substitutes playing in the second-half exhibit increased heart rates compared with full-match players (84% vs 81% maximum heart rate); however, this remains lower than the first-half heart rate responses of full-match players (84% vs 86% maximum heart rate).
CONCLUSIONS: This systematic scoping review summarises current evidence and key findings relating to the internal and external characteristics of soccer substitutes during warm-up, match play and training that can be used in practice to inform player welfare and sport science support within these cohorts. Chiefly, during match-day warm-ups, soccer substitutes' body temperature and physical performance responses may not be maintained, despite typical substitute-specific match-day practices being employed. Similarly, soccer substitutes were frequently reported to demonstrate higher relative total distance, high-speed running and sprinting outputs compared with starting players. Further research is needed to better understand performance demands, longitudinal adaptations, contextual influences and female-specific responses in soccer substitutes.

title: Evolution of Reverse Shoulder Arthroplasty: Two Decades of Evidence from the Journal of Shoulder and Elbow Surgery.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Reverse shoulder arthroplasty (rTSA) has evolved from a salvage procedure to a widely adopted reconstructive solution. This study performed a descriptive bibliometric and content-trend analysis of rTSA publications in the Journal of Shoulder and Elbow Surgery (JSES) from 2004-2025.
METHODS: A systematic review identified 506 clinical rTSA studies published in JSES between 2004 and 2025. Extracted variables included publication year, level of evidence, authorship, institution, geographic origin, research topic, demographics, indications, complications, and implant characteristics. Temporal trends were tested using Mann-Kendall trend test and segmented regression; the relationship between implant design representation and complication reporting was evaluated with Spearman rank correlation.
RESULTS: Annual publications increased significantly (BH-adjusted P < .001), peaking at 51 studies in 2023. Mean level of evidence improved (BH-adjusted P < .001), from 4.0 (2006) to 2.86 (2023). Early authorship centered on foundational surgeons (Frankle, Boileau, Walch) and European institutions, later diffusing globally. Mean age rose modestly, though this did not remain significant after correction for multiple comparisons (BH-adjusted P = .077), stabilizing near 70-72 years after 2012. Research focus shifted from complications/technique toward outcomes after 2013, then toward instrumentation, rehabilitation, and cost. Osteoarthritis indications increased (BH-adjusted P = .005) while revision surgery declined (BH-adjusted P = .002). Implant design shifted from medialized to lateralized/non-Grammont configurations (both BH-adjusted P < .001). No individual complication subtype showed a significant temporal trend.
CONCLUSION: RTSA publication trends in JSES reflect the field's evolution from complication-focused study to evidence-driven refinement. Implant design, evidence level, and indications changed significantly, alongside, but not statistically linked to, complication reporting, informing future shoulder reconstruction research directions.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Literature Review, Bibliometric Analysis.

title: Age-Related Patterns of Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs) Symptoms and Key Performance Factors in Adolescent Biathletes.
abstract: Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs) impairs health and performance, but age-related patterns in its emergence remain unclear. This study examines RED symptoms in adolescent biathletes at season-start and their link to end-of-season performance. A national cross-sectional study including prospective performance registration recruited biathletes to complete validated questionnaires, followed by clinical interviews if eating disorders (EDs) were indicated. Athletes ≥ 18 years were invited for physical laboratory assessments. End-of-season results were retrieved from open records. Analyses were performed by elastic net regression to identify the most stable predictors of performance, which were finally included in a linear regression model. Seventy-two athletes (55% females) with mean (SD) age 17.8 (1.4) years, 13.3 (3.3) training hours/week, and representing median (min, max) tier 3.0 (2, 5) were included. Prevalence in symptoms of low energy availability (LEA) was 18%, REDs 32%, EDs 11% (20% among females), and of depression 15%. Among 28 athletes (43% female) completing laboratory assessments, 11% had low BMD and ≤ 25% had clinical metabolic markers. Symptoms of mental health issues and REDs were more common in females and the older age groups. Higher training volume and low RED severity positively predicted performance, whereas injury/illness-related training absences, cholesterol, and body fat percentage negatively affected race results. RED symptoms are common in young biathletes. Illness/injury-related training absences were frequent and linked to poorer end-of-season performance, underscoring the need for routine screening by health- and performance teams to detect and manage early symptoms of LEA, reduce RED risk, and prevent premature career termination.

title: Surgery under fire: war injuries and the consequences of delayed care in Ethiopia's Tigray region.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The armed conflict in Ethiopia, particularly in the Tigray region, has caused a substantial burden of war-related injuries in the context of a fragile and disrupted health system. Restricted access to timely surgical care has resulted in delayed presentation and may contribute to secondary complications, contractures, peripheral nerve dysfunction, and long-term disability. However, the consequences of delayed surgical treatment for conflict-related extremity trauma in active war settings remain insufficiently described. This study aimed to characterize conflict-related injuries in Mek'ele, Ethiopia, with a particular focus on delayed surgical care, peripheral nerve injuries, and reconstructive needs.
METHODS: This retrospective observational study was conducted between September and December 2023 at Ayder Comprehensive Specialized Hospital in Mek'ele, the capital city of Ethiopia's Tigray region. Patients presenting with conflict-related injuries were identified through routine clinical documentation. Epidemiological characteristics, prior surgical interventions, presenting complaints, clinical findings, and diagnoses were recorded. Peripheral nerve injuries and reconstructive challenges were analyzed in detail. Surgical treatment plans were categorized into reconstructive, corrective and functional, tendon and muscle, nerve, scar and contracture, limb or tissue removal, and supportive procedures. Group comparisons were performed using chi-square and Fisher's exact tests, and logistic regression models were used to estimate relative likelihoods. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05.
RESULTS: A total of 197 conflict-related injuries were analyzed, including 108 bullet injuries (54.8%) and 82 blast injuries (41.6%). Peripheral nerve injuries were identified in 54.3% of patients. Bullet injuries were more strongly associated with movement restriction, functional deficits, and peripheral nerve damage, whereas blast injuries were more frequently linked to fractures, soft tissue defects, pain, and scars or wounds. Blast injuries more often required reconstructive procedures and contracture release, while bullet injuries more frequently required corrective and functional surgery. Because most patients presented months to years after injury, primary nerve repair was rarely feasible, resulting in a high demand for secondary salvage procedures such as tendon transfers and muscle transpositions.
CONCLUSIONS: Conflict-related extremity trauma in Tigray is characterized not only by injury mechanism but also by the consequences of delayed access to surgical care. Missed opportunities for early definitive treatment contributed to a high burden of peripheral nerve deficits, contractures, reconstructive needs, and long-term functional impairment. Improving access to acute trauma care, early nerve repair, reconstructive surgery, and rehabilitation is essential to reduce disability in conflict-affected settings.

title: Effects of Whey Protein Supplementation on Muscle Damage, Hepatic Stress, and Inflammatory Markers in Power- and Endurance-Trained Athletes.
abstract: This study investigated the effects of 8 weeks of whey protein supplementation (30 g/day) on biomarkers of liver function, inflammation, and muscle damage in trained power-trained (predominantly speed-power/anaerobic-power disciplines) and endurance-trained athletes, in a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled design. Fifty-nine male athletes were stratified into power (n = 30) and endurance (n = 29) groups, then randomly assigned to a whey protein group (WG) or a placebo control group (CG). Biomarkers assessed pre- and post-intervention included alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), C-reactive protein (CRP), and creatine kinase (CK). Significant reductions in ALT, AST, and CK were observed in both endurance- and power-trained athletes after supplementation (p = 0.001, p = 0.015, p = 0.001, and p = 0.003 respectively), indicating attenuated hepatic and muscular stress. Among the four biomarkers, only ALT displayed a statistically significant three-way interaction (Time × Supplementation × Training modality; p = 0.003), identifying it as the sole marker showing a genuine modality-specific differential response to supplementation. A significant within-group reduction in CRP was additionally observed in the supplemented power-trained athletes (p = 0.039), whereas endurance athletes showed only minor, non-significant changes; because the omnibus three-way interaction for CRP was not significant, this finding is reported as a within-group trend rather than evidence of a differential effect between modalities. Placebo groups demonstrated stable or increased enzyme and CRP values, particularly in endurance athletes. These findings suggest that whey protein may attenuate exercise-induced hepatic and muscular stress across training modalities, with a modality-specific effect on hepatic stress markers (ALT) observed in power-trained athletes. The results highlight whey protein's potential as a nutritional aid to promote recovery and physiological adaptation, possibly mediated by antioxidant and anti-inflammatory mechanisms. Further studies are warranted to examine long-term outcomes and dose-response effects across different training profiles.
