title: Additive effects of active vitamin D3 or vitamin E administration on therapeutic lower-limb home exercise for knee osteoarthritis: A pilot prospective randomized controlled trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Quadriceps weakness, inflammation, and reduced physical function are common in knee osteoarthritis (OA), and lower limb exercise therapy is an established non-pharmacological treatment. Vitamin D3 (vit D3) and vitamin E (vit E) have been proposed as adjunctive therapies; however, clinical findings are inconsistent. We aimed to examine whether combining lower limb home exercises with oral active vit D3 or vit E supplementation provides additive benefits compared with home exercise alone in women with symptomatic knee OA.
METHODS: Eighty-eight postmenopausal women with knee OA (Kellgren-Lawrence grade 2-4; 71.9 ± 5.6 years) were randomly assigned to receive therapeutic lower limb home exercise only, home exercise with active vit D3 administration, or home exercise with vit E administration. Participants performed isometric lower limb exercises twice daily for 24 weeks. Subsequently, they were assessed using the Japanese knee osteoarthritis measure (JKOM) as the primary outcome. Secondary outcomes were short-form health survey, grip strength, quadriceps muscle strength, 10-m walk test, inflammatory markers, bone mineral density, and body composition. For data analyses, we used paired and independent t tests, analysis of variance, and analysis of covariance, adjusting for age, body mass index, and Kellgren-Lawrence grade.
RESULTS: Eighty participants completed follow-up. All groups showed significant improvements in JKOM score, quadriceps muscle strength, and 10-m walk test. Grip strength improved significantly only in the group that received active vit D. No significant between-group differences were observed in JKOM scores, short-form health survey-36, muscle strength, or physical performance. Inflammatory markers decreased significantly in the vit E group, although between-group differences were not observed. No other significant between-group differences were found, except in bone mineral density.
CONCLUSIONS: Administering active vit D3 or vit E for 24 weeks as an adjunct to lower limb home exercises did not yield significant additive effects on symptoms, muscle strength, or physical performance in women with knee OA. Exercise therapy alone remained effective, and vitamin supplementation showed nutrient-specific trends.

title: The Effect of Acute Beetroot Juice and Caffeine Supplementation on Specific Judo Performance During a Simulated Competition Day in Judo Athletes.
abstract: Beetroot juice (BJ) and caffeine (CAF) are well-established ergogenic aids for exercise performance. However, little is known about their efficacy and interaction within the specific context of a judo competition day. This study investigated the acute effects of BJ, CAF, and their combination (BJCAF) on judo-specific performance across a simulated competition day. Using a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover design, 35 competitive judo athletes (age 23 ± 5 years; body mass 74 ± 13 kg) completed 4 sessions (BJ, CAF, BJCAF, and placebo), each consisting of 5 trials of judo randori and a Special Judo Fitness Test (SJFT), followed by neuromuscular and cognitive assessments. Compared with placebo, CAF enhanced SJFT performance, neuromuscular function, and cognition in trials 1-3 but not in trial 5 (p < 0.05). Conversely, BJ improved these same metrics in trial 5 (p < 0.05). BJCAF enhanced SJFT performance across trials 1-3 and 5, cognitive functions in trials 1, 2, and 4, and neuromuscular performance in all trials (p < 0.05). Importantly, in trial 5, both BJ and BJCAF conditions yielded improved SJFT performance, neuromuscular function, and cognitive outcomes compared to CAF alone (p < 0.05). The results demonstrate that the ergogenic effect of CAF was not maintained throughout the simulated competition day, whereas BJ provided late-stage benefits. Co-ingestion effectively counteracted the later-session decline observed with CAF alone while maintaining its early advantages. This highlights the importance of considering temporal dynamics and metabolic costs when designing nutritional strategies for multi-bout, high-intensity sports tournaments such as judo.

title: Discussing pain increases at the point of exercise prescription: a clinical commentary for persistent musculoskeletal conditions.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Patients with persistent musculoskeletal pain frequently perform prescribed exercise without direct supervision. When exercise increases symptoms, patients may be uncertain whether to continue, modify the session, or seek advice. A prescription that specifies exercises and dosage but provides no guidance about possible symptom aggravation may therefore leave an important gap in preparation.
PURPOSE: This commentary proposes that, when prescribed exercise may increase pain, the possible response should be discussed at the point of prescription and that clinicians should prepare patients for how symptom aggravation will be interpreted and reviewed.
DISCUSSION AND RECOMMENDATIONS: Trials comparing painful and nonpainful exercise, including an updated 2025 systematic review, show no consistent advantage for either approach and provide no basis for a universal adjustment rule. Pain-monitoring protocols developed for Achilles tendinopathy indicate that continued loading can be compatible with recovery in that condition, but their thresholds have not been validated for other presentations and should not be transferred by default. Features of altered nociceptive processing may further complicate interpretation of symptom aggravation but do not remove the need for assessment. What is proposed is a conversation rather than an algorithm: an explicit discussion, established when exercise is prescribed, about what a symptom increase might mean, how it will be interpreted, and when and how the plan will be reviewed. The evidence considered spans low back pain, osteoarthritis, and tendinopathy; extension to other persistent musculoskeletal conditions remains a reasonable but untested proposition.
CONCLUSION: Research should establish what instructions clinicians currently provide when exercise increases pain, whether patients understand them, and which responses lead patients to continue, modify, or abandon exercise. Future studies should also determine whether discussing possible aggravation before it occurs improves adherence, confidence, function, and timely reassessment.

title: Conceptual Frameworks and Assessment of Readiness to Train in Endurance Exercise: A Systematic Review.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Readiness to train has emerged as a construct to guide daily training prescription and recovery management in endurance athletes. However, its conceptual basis, assessment, and methodological quality and validity remain inconsistently defined. This systematic review aimed to (1) identify how readiness is defined in endurance exercise and (2) categorize tools used to assess it. As a secondary aim, the review evaluated the methodological approach of the studies employing these tools.
METHODS: Following PRISMA guidelines, PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were explored. Eligible studies included endurance athletes aged 18-65 years, evaluating readiness before or after training or competition. Two reviewers independently screened, extracted data, and assessed quality using the revised Cochrane Risk of Bias tool. Fourteen studies were included.
RESULTS: Readiness definitions were inconsistent and frequently overlapped with related constructs such as recovery and fatigue. Ten studies used self-reported tools (fatigue, sleep, stress, and soreness). Nine studies assessed objective tools, including heart rate (HR) variability, resting HR, countermovement jump, and submaximal tests. HR variability-based approaches and individualized feedback were used to track autonomic recovery and guide training prescription, while on-field indices (eg, HR-running speed, HR-running power, countermovement jump) provided neuromuscular insights, although they can also be influenced by cardiovascular and metabolic factors. Overall, there was considerable heterogeneity in tools and their combinations, highlighting the lack of standardized approaches to assess readiness to train. Seven studies combined subjective and objective measures, suggesting a more comprehensive monitoring strategy. However, many of these tools were primarily used to assess related constructs (eg, fatigue, recovery, and training adaptation) rather than directly predict performance; consequently, their ability to predict performance outcomes remained limited or was not even assessed.
CONCLUSION: This review highlights substantial conceptual ambiguity, methodological limitations, and heterogeneity in readiness assessment. A multidimensional framework conceptualizing readiness as a dynamic psychophysiological state influenced by stress, recovery, and contextual factors may support more structured and meaningful monitoring in endurance athletes.

title: Predicting Return to Play After Achilles Tendon Injury in National Football League Players Using Machine Learning.
abstract:
UNLABELLED: BackgroundNational Football League (NFL) players frequently experience Achilles tendon (AT) injuries. However, there is mixed evidence regarding factors influencing return to play (RTP) after AT injury. The objective of this study is to develop machine learning models to predict NFL players' likelihood of RTP within 1 year of an AT tear.
HYPOTHESIS: Machine learning models can predict 1-year RTP status in NFL players following AT tear.
STUDY DESIGN: Retrospective Cohort.MethodsA retrospective review was conducted to identify NFL players who sustained unilateral AT injuries from 2004 to 2024. Player demographics and performance data were recorded. Return to play was defined as generating playing statistics. Five machine learning models were developed: logistic regression, random forest classifier, XGBoost, Gaussian naive Bayes, and K-nearest neighbors. Accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 were used to assess model performance.ResultsOne hundred seventy-six NFL players were identified with an AT injury. One hundred eight players achieved RTP within 1 year (class 1), while 63 players did not (class 0). In the full cohort, injury etiology was the most influential feature associated with 1-year RTP, followed by pre-injury performance. Among the 99 players with a confirmed AT tear, 48 players achieved RTP within 1 year (class 1), while 51 players did not (class 0). Within the confirmed-tear cohort, draft round and games started were the leading predictors of 1-year RTP, which was best predicted by random forest with a mean accuracy of 0.69, precision of 0.68, recall of 0.70, and an F1-score of 0.69 for class 0.ConclusionMachine learning models that combine clinical and performance metrics of NFL athletes demonstrated potential for predicting 1-year RTP after AT injury and identifying factors associated with RTP.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Machine learning could be integrated into clinical decision-making and prognosis to refine rehabilitation approaches in NFL players.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 3.

title: Objective Return-to-Sport (RTS) Decision Frameworks for Adolescent Shoulder and Elbow Injuries: Tests, Thresholds and Exercise Targets.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Adolescent shoulder and elbow injuries are increasing due to sports specialization and year-round training, yet return-to-sport decisions typically rely on adult-derived heuristics that fail to address the unique physiology, growth plate vulnerability, and recovery needs of developing athletes aged 10-19 years.
OBJECTIVE: This review proposes a novel, objective three-pillar RTS framework integrating: (1) foundational tissue capacity, (2) dynamic movement quality and neuromuscular control, and (3) sport-specific load tolerance. We synthesize current evidence to establish provisional, consensus-based adolescent thresholds and provide a practical bedside toolkit for immediate clinical implementation.
METHODS: We conducted a narrative synthesis of contemporary original evidence, consensus recommendations, and validation studies relevant to adolescent shoulder and elbow rehabilitation. Evidence was critically appraised for youth-specific validation, with explicit distinction between evidence-based interventions and emerging aspirational technologies requiring prospective adolescent cohort validation.
RESULTS: We propose a hybrid benchmarking model combining limb symmetry indices (LSI ≥90%) with population-referenced percentiles (≥25th percentile for age/sex/sport) as provisional, consensus-based thresholds. A three-stage progression is outlined: Clinic-ready (pain-free ROM, isometric IR/ER LSI ≥90%), Training-ready (dynamic rotational LSI ≥90%, preserved scapular kinematics), and Game-ready (sport-specific tolerance with 5% velocity loss during simulated exposure). We provide a low-resource bedside toolkit including belt-stabilized hand-held dynamometry, Closed Kinetic Chain Upper Extremity Stability Test (CKCUEST), Push-Up Plus, Athletic Shoulder positions, seated medicine-ball throw, and simple interval tolerance simulations with specific protocols and thresholds. A stepwise algorithm advances from capacity → movement quality → load tolerance with targeted remediation at each gate.
CONCLUSION: Moving beyond time-based or adult-derived heuristics, this objective multidimensional framework aligns tissue recovery with sport-specific demands through quantifiable metrics. While provisional thresholds require further adolescent validation, the framework offers an evidence-guided pathway that mitigates reinjury risk, restores performance, and supports safe reintegration into sport. Implementation requires adolescent-specific normative databases, stakeholder communication, and cost-effective technological integration for equitable adoption.

title: Muscle biomechanical rehabilitation following therapy in Achilles and patellar tendinopathy assessed by MR elastography.
abstract: Tendon healing is the primary goal of tendinopathy therapy. However, the therapeutic response of adjacent muscles remains uninvestigated. MR-elastography (MRE) can assess muscle biomechanical properties and function. This study investigated muscle biomechanical responses in patients treated for patellar (PT) or Achilles tendinopathy (AT). A prospective longitudinal study included 20 athletes, 8 with AT (41 years ± 8; 6 men) and 12 with PT (34 years ± 10; 12 men), who underwent MRI, diffusion-tensor-imaging (DTI), and MRE before and ≥6 months post-treatment. Isotropic (ciso) and anisotropic stiffness parameters (c‖ and c⊥) in tendon-adjacent muscles were derived and analyzed between groups and longitudinally compared with clinical scores and tendon dimensions. At baseline, symptomatic legs with higher tendon dimensions and clinical symptoms exhibited lower muscle stiffness than asymptomatic legs (p<0.05). Post-treatment, AT patients showed increased ciso (4.3±8.5%) in gastrocnemius and posterior soleus (SolP; 4.9±8.6%) in treated legs but decreased SolP stiffness (-3.2±7.2%) in untreated legs (p<0.05). In PT patients, only anisotropic MRE (c‖: 5.3±15.2% and c⊥: 10.3±12.7%) in vastus lateralis showed significant increases (p<0.05) post-treatment. In treated legs of AT and PT, increased muscle stiffness post-treatment correlated negatively with tendon dimensions (p<0.05). Post-therapy, tendon-adjacent muscles exhibited increased stiffness in affected leg and decreased stiffness in contralateral leg (particularly SolP), potentially reflecting altered muscle use and loading, respectively. The observed changes in muscle stiffness may help characterize muscle biomechanical changes during rehabilitation and balanced recovery. Furthermore, anisotropic muscle stiffness was more sensitive to tendon structural changes than isotropic stiffness, warranting further validation for clinical assessment.

title: Orthobiologics in Focus: Current Evidence, Clinical Applications, and Future Directions, A Scoping Review.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Regenerative modalities are increasingly becoming part of orthopedic practice with the use of orthobiologic interventions. These interventions make use of biological approaches to help in repairing the tissues, mitigating nociception, and improving locomotor performance.
OBJECTIVE: The current scoping review is a review of the modern literature as of 2020-2025 on orthobiologic therapies. It examines their clinical effectiveness, the strength of supporting evidence, and the development of new progress in musculoskeletal pathology regenerative management.
METHODS: A systematic search in PubMed, Scopus, Embase, and WoS was done on the articles with their indexes dated between January 2020 and February 2025. The inclusion criteria were human and animal studies that utilized platelet-rich plasma (PRP), (MSCs), bone marrow aspirate concentrate (BMAC), and adipose-derived products strategies using a scaffold only. Synthesis and data extraction were conducted as per PRISMA-ScR standards.
RESULTS: Among the 1716 records that had been filtered, 81 studies met inclusion criteria. Most of them were randomized or comparative trials (77% Level I-II evidence), which are evidence of the high methodological quality. PRP was the most commonly researched modality, whereas MSC-based interventions were the most common.
CONCLUSION: PRP, MSCs, and BMAC are orthobiologic modalities, which are evidence-based and effective alternatives to promote musculoskeletal healing and regeneration. These interventions supplemented by conventional surgical procedures and rehabilitative interventions yield pain relief, functional restoration, and long-term joint maintenance in a spectrum of orthopedic complications.

title: [Disordered eating behaviors and eating disorders among athletes II.].
abstract: Over the past two and a half decades, a substantial shift has occurred in the understanding of disordered eating and eating disorders among athletes. Research has gradually moved beyond the concept of the female athlete triad towards the model of relative energy deficiency in sport (REDs), which recognizes low energy availability as a key factor affecting both athletes' health and performance. The aim of this study is to review the international literature published between 2000 and 2025 on disordered eating and eating disorders in athletes, with particular emphasis on prevalence, the contemporary interpretation of risk factors, the development of the REDs concept, and current recommendations for screening, treatment, and prevention. A thematic narrative literature review was conducted using the PubMed, ScienceDirect, and Scopus databases. Publications and professional consensus statements addressing disordered eating, eating disorders, relative energy deficiency, screening, prevention, and multidisciplinary care in athletes were included in the analysis. The reviewed literature indicates that disordered eating behaviors are considerably more prevalent than clinically diagnosed eating disorders; however, both conditions adversely affect athletes' health and performance. The evidence also confirms that low energy availability is not exclusively associated with eating disorders but may also result from an imbalance between energy intake and exercise expenditure. The introduction of the REDs model substantially expanded the earlier female athlete triad concept by highlighting the involvement of male athletes, the role of psychological factors, and the multisystem consequences of low energy availability. Current international recommendations emphasize early identification, sport-specific risk assessment, and multidisciplinary care as the cornerstones of effective prevention and treatment. Contemporary approaches to nutrition-related problems in athletes consider disordered eating, eating disorders, and relative energy deficiency as interrelated conditions. The development of standardized multidisciplinary models of care consistent with current international recommendations would be warranted in Hungary. Orv Hetil. 2026; 167(42): 1702-1709.

title: Short-term effects of extracorporeal shockwave therapy and low-level laser therapy on clinical outcomes and ultrasonographic tendon thickness in lateral elbow tendinopathy.
abstract: BackgroundThis study aimed to compare the short-term effects of extracorporeal shock wave therapy (ESWT) and low-level laser therapy (LLLT) on pain, elbow function, health-related quality of life, hand grip strength, and ultrasonographic extensor tendon thickness in patients with LET.ObjectiveIn this prospective, randomized, controlled, single-blind trial, patients with LET were randomly assigned to either ESWT or LLLT. Both groups received the same standardized home exercise program and lateral epicondylitis brace. Visual Analog Scale (VAS), the Patient-Rated Tennis Elbow Evaluation (PRTEE), Short Form-36 (SF-36), hand grip strength, and ultrasonographic evaluation were assessed before and after three weeks of randomisation.ResultsAt three weeks, the ESWT group demonstrated significantly lower post-treatment pain intensity (VAS) than the LLLT group (p = 0.004). ESWT was also associated with significantly better outcomes in PRTEE pain scores (p = 0.030), ultrasonographic tendon thickness (p = 0.021), and the Role Physical (p = 0.029) and General Health (p = 0.005) domains of the SF-36. No significant between-group differences were observed in hand grip strength, PRTEE function, PRTEE total score, or the remaining SF-36 domains.ConclusionWhen used as adjuncts to a standardized exercise program and LET brace, ESWT was associated with greater short-term pain reduction and more favorable outcomes in the PRTEE pain subscale, ultrasonographic tendon thickness, and selected domains of health-related quality of life compared with LLLT. These findings suggest that ESWT may offer greater short-term pain-related benefits than LLLT when both are added to exercise and bracing.

title: Insertional Achilles tendinopathy State of pathology: Insertional tendon tendinopathies.
abstract: Insertional Achilles tendinopathy (IAT) is a common but disabling pathology affecting both athletes and older subjects. The aim of the present study was to provide a practical review of IA, addressing the following questions: What are the etiologies and pathophysiology? Etiology is multifactorial, involving anatomic aspects and especially posterosuperior calcaneal prominence, biomechanical aspects such as short triceps surae, pes cavus or hindfoot varus, extrinsic aspects of footwear and overtraining, and metabolic aspects. Pathophysiology, depending on the individual case, implicates true insertional tendinopathy and posterior bone-tendon impingement to varying degrees, often with pre-Achilles bursitis; the distinction is crucial to decision-making. Impingement or enthesopathy lead to progressive disorganization of the collagen matrix, pathologic neovascularization and mucoid degeneration of the tendon, often with intratendon calcifications and inflammatory retrocalcaneal bursitis. How to establish diagnosis? Diagnosis is primarily clinical, based on pain location, which is median in case of insertional tendinopathy and more lateral in case of posterior impingement with bursitis. Examination finds pain on palpation of the Achilles insertion, sometimes with local thickening, posterior tumefaction and painful restriction of ankle dorsiflexion. Tensing the tendon typically reproduces the pain. Functional tests may show restriction due to pain, without tendon tear. Weight-bearing X-ray, ultrasound and especially MRI analyze the respective roles of bone, tendon and bursa injury; weight-bearing CT can be contributive in some morphologically complex situations. Ultrasound reveals tendon thickening, hypoechogenic degenerative areas, hypervascularization on Doppler and associated bursitis. MRI shows lesion extension: intratendon degeneration, deep fiber involvement and retrocalcaneal inflammation. What are the non-operative treatments? Initial treatment is conservative, based on adapting weight-bearing and footwear, with exercises adapted to the form of the insertion, extracorporeal shock waves and rehabilitation. What are the surgical options and their expected results? In case of failure of well-conducted non-operative treatment, surgical strategy depends on lesion type, degree of posterior impingement, degree of tendon degeneration and degree of triceps surae stiffness. Expected results comprise pain relief, functional improvement on VISA-A score, and progressive return to activities, with timing depending on the technique and the initial level of activity. How to choose the surgical treatment? Surgical options comprise bone decompression, debridement and tendon reinsertion, flexor hallucis longus transfer and gastrocnemius lengthening depending on lesion type on clinical examination and imaging.

title: Platelet-related extracellular vesicles: Therapeutic roles in musculoskeletal disorders.
abstract: Musculoskeletal disorders are a major cause of pain, disability, and loss of function. Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) has been widely investigated for musculoskeletal repair, and interest has increasingly extended to extracellular vesicle (EV) preparations obtained from platelet-related starting materials. These include EV-enriched preparations collected from isolated platelets or defined platelet concentrates (P-EVs), from PRP (PRP-EVs), and from platelet lysate (PL-EVs). They do not represent the same biological product. Their cellular contributors, co-isolated soluble components, and molecular composition can differ substantially, and the name of the starting material does not prove the origin of every vesicle in the preparation. Preclinical studies nevertheless suggest that these EV preparations can influence inflammatory responses, cartilage metabolism, tendon-cell behavior, and the local repair environment. The strength of this evidence varies with the source material, separation and characterization methods, experimental model, and delivery strategy. This review examines the therapeutic evidence for platelet-related EV preparations in musculoskeletal disorders, while keeping P-EVs, PRP-EVs, PL-EVs, and plasma-derived EVs distinct and considering the methodological limitations that currently restrict comparison and clinical translation.

title: A Narrative Review of Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction Graft Choice and Its Influence on Return to Sport.
abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) rupture is among the most common knee injuries in active individuals and can lead to persistent instability, secondary intra-articular damage, and an elevated risk of osteoarthritis. Because return to sport (RTS) is a major goal for most active patients and graft selection remains one of the most debated aspects of ACL reconstruction, this narrative review summarizes the contemporary evidence on how graft choice influences RTS, focusing on the four most common grafts: bone-patellar tendon-bone (BTB), hamstring tendon (HT), quadriceps tendon (QT), and allograft.
RECENT FINDINGS: RTS rates range from ~ 65% to 73% at three years and are higher (83-90%) in elite and high-school athletes. In young, active patients, autografts are associated with higher RTS and lower revision rates than allografts, and high-level evidence-including randomized-trial meta-analyses-has not established the superiority of any single autograft. BTB offers reliable bone-to-bone healing and low revision rates; HT reduces donor-site morbidity and anterior knee pain but has variable diameter and possible flexion weakness; and QT is a versatile option with favorable biomechanics, low donor-site morbidity, and encouraging RTS data, including in skeletally immature athletes. RTS is one of several important outcomes after ACL reconstruction, alongside long-term joint health and reinjury prevention. For RTS, the literature supports autograft over allograft in young, active patients while identifying no universally superior autograft. Graft selection should be individualized to patient age, sport, activity level, anatomy, and reinjury risk; the senior author favors QT or BTB autografts for high-demand athletes.

title: Calf Injuries: Anatomy, Pathology, and Treatment.
abstract: Calf injuries are common in athletes and typically result in missed time from sport and activities of daily living. The three individual triceps surae muscles can be injured, with differing described mechanisms. Gastrocnemius or plantaris strains tend to occur during sudden explosive movement of the ankle from a dorsiflexed to a plantarflexed position with the knee in extension. Soleus strains typically occur from repetitive dorsiflexion of the ankle with the knee flexed. Imaging modalities such as magnetic resonance imaging and ultrasonography can be helpful in determining the location and grade of injury, which can aid in treatment and return to play timelines. Classically, these injuries have been graded as grade I, II, or III, with grade I having <10% muscle fiber disruption, grade II having >10 to 50% muscle fiber disruption, and grade III having 50 to 100% muscle fiber disruption. The mainstay of treatment for most calf strains is nonsurgical, with surgical management being rare but reported in the literature for isolated grade III ruptures of the medial head of the gastrocnemius. Return to sport and activities requires a graduated physical therapy program focused on restoring tissue length without excessive strain. Recent limited evidence has shown promising results with quicker return to activities and decreased pain with platelet-rich plasma injections.

title: Low Physical Therapy Referral Rates for Knee Osteoarthritis Present a Barrier to Care for Patients With Medicaid.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the rates of physical therapy (PT) referral for knee osteoarthritis (KOA) and factors associated with referral patterns, including insurance status, provider specialty, year, and patient demographics and comorbidities.
DESIGN: This retrospective cohort study included 41,373 patients diagnosed with KOA at an integrated health system in Arizona and Colorado, USA between January 2020 and February 2023. PT referral rates were stratified by insurance type. Multivariable logistic regression assessed predictors of referral including insurance type, age, BMI, sex, race/ethnicity, provider specialty, year of visit, and comorbidities.
RESULTS: Crude PT referral rates at the initial visit were 12.06% for Medicaid, 6.83% for Medicare, 10.29% for commercial insurance, and 8.33% for uninsured patients. Adjusted analysis showed that Medicaid patients had higher referral odds (OR, 1.20; 95% CI [1.10, 1.30]; p < 0.001), whereas Medicare patients had lower odds (OR, 0.76; 95% CI [0.66, 0.88]; p < 0.001) compared to those with commercial insurance. Female (OR, 1.21; 95% CI [1.14, 1.29]; p < 0.001) and Hispanic patients (OR 1.18; 95% CI [1.09, 1.29]; p < 0.001) demonstrated increased referral odds. Provider specialty was associated with PT referral, with non-operative sports medicine providers having the highest referral odds (OR, 3.00; 95% CI [2.72, 3.31]; p < 0.001) relative to orthopaedic surgery.
CONCLUSION: Despite strong clinical practice guidelines recommending PT, formal referral rates for patients with KOA remain low regardless of insurance type, patient characteristics, and referring healthcare provider specialty. Low formal PT referral rates may represent a barrier to evidence-based KOA care.

title: Attention allocation in team sports: A systematic review and meta-analysis based on eye-tracking.
abstract: Expert athletes are generally considered to exhibit distinct visual search behaviors and superior behavioral performance. However, findings regarding perceptual-cognitive differences across skill levels in team sports remain inconsistent. Therefore, this study aimed to systematically examine differences in visual search behavior and behavioral performance across skill levels in team sports. A systematic search was conducted in EBSCO, PubMed, Scopus, SPORTDiscus, and Web of Science, resulting in 26 eligible studies involving expert, intermediate, and novice athletes from football, basketball, and volleyball. A random-effects meta-analysis was performed using Hedges' g to estimate pooled effect sizes, and subgroup analyses were conducted to examine potential moderating factors. Results revealed that, for eye movement outcomes, only limited evidence supported a significant pooled effect for fixation duration across skill levels. Subgroup analyses based on a limited number of studies identified significant differences between intermediate and novice athletes, particularly in the number of fixations in basketball and volleyball. For behavioral performance, significant differences were observed in reaction time for expert-intermediate and expert-novice comparisons, whereas the overall effect for performance accuracy was not significant after publication bias adjustment. These findings suggest a complex relationship between visual characteristics and behavioral performance at different skill levels in team sports.

title: Associations of cardiac autonomic modulation and urinary adrenal hormones with marathon finishing time in middle-aged male athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The autonomic nervous and endocrine systems are involved in the physiological adaptation to exercise, and in experimental settings both the sympathovagal balance and the adrenal function are associated with athletic performance. In this real-life field study, the association between non-invasive markers of cardiac autonomic modulation, urinary adrenal hormone levels, and marathon finishing time in middle-aged Caucasian male athletes was investigated.
METHODS: A prospective study was conducted in male marathon runners aged ≥30 years. Continuous single-lead electrocardiographic (ECG) recordings were obtained using a wearable chest device from the day before the marathon until after its completion. Urinary adrenal hormone levels were measured before and after the race. Univariate linear regression analyses were performed to correlate general characteristics, nocturnal heart rate variability (HRV) parameters, and hormonal parameters with marathon finishing time. A multivariable model was then applied including age, body mass index (BMI), and training hours.
RESULTS: 104 athletes were enrolled in the study and 73 (median age 48 years, interquartile range = 16) had adequate data quality for the final analysis. Several HRV parameters correlated with better performance at univariate analysis; lower minimum nocturnal heart rate and vagal predominance, expressed as higher 2 Like Variations (2LV) values remained independently associated with shorter finishing time. Among hormonal variables, the post-/pre-race ratio of urinary normetanephrine hourly output and cortisol/cortisone ratio remained significant at multivariable analysis. Only BMI, but not age and training history, remained significant in a model integrating HRV and hormones.
CONCLUSIONS: Under real-world marathon conditions, specific HRV indices and endocrine markers showed promising value as indicators of physiological readiness with endurance exercise in male master athletes.

title: Longitudinal Serum Biomarker Profiles of Inflammation and Cartilage Matrix Metabolism During the First Year After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury initiates biological processes linked to joint tissue degeneration. The longitudinal time course of serum biomarkers reflecting inflammation and cartilage metabolism after ACL reconstruction (ACLR), particularly in comparison with uninjured controls, has not been characterized across the first postoperative year.
HYPOTHESIS: Inflammatory (monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 [MCP-1]) and degradative (matrix metalloproteinase-3 [MMP-3]) biomarker concentrations would be elevated pre-ACLR and decrease over time, whereas cartilage turnover biomarker concentrations (cartilage oligomeric matrix protein [COMP] and type II collagen degradation-to-synthesis ratio [C2C:CPII]) would increase postoperatively. Also, pre-ACLR biomarker concentrations would be associated with concentrations at 6 and 12 months post-ACLR.
STUDY DESIGN: Cohort study; Level of evidence, 2.
METHODS: A total of 33 individuals with ACL injuries (52% female; mean age, 20.8 ± 2.4 years) were evaluated pre-ACLR and at 6 and 12 months post-ACLR. A total of 33 matched uninjured controls were included. Serum concentrations of MCP-1, MMP-3, COMP, and C2C:CPII were assessed using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays. Linear mixed-effects models with model-based contrasts were used to evaluate differences across groups and time points. ACLR-only linear mixed-effects regression models were used to assess associations between pre-ACLR and follow-up biomarker concentrations. Exploratory post hoc models evaluated differences by concomitant injury status.
RESULTS: MCP-1 was elevated in individuals with ACL injuries compared with controls at all ACLR time points (all Padj < .001), with no change across ACLR time points. MMP-3 increased from pre-ACLR to 6 months post-ACLR (Padj < .001) but did not differ from controls at any time point. COMP was consistently greater in individuals with ACL injuries than in controls at all time points (all Padj≤ .021), with no changes across ACLR time points. C2C:CPII was greater at 12 months post-ACLR than at pre-ACLR and 6 months post-ACLR (both Padj < .001) and than in uninjured controls (Padj = .001). Pre-ACLR MCP-1, MMP-3, and COMP concentrations were associated with concentrations at both 6 and 12 months post-ACLR (all P≤ .006), whereas C2C:CPII was associated only with 12-month concentrations (P = .018).
CONCLUSION: Inflammatory and cartilage-related biomarkers remain altered throughout the first year after ACLR, suggesting that the biological response is not fully resolved by reconstruction and standard rehabilitation but extends beyond the early postoperative period.

title: A Practical Pipeline for Patient-Specific Musculoskeletal Modeling: A Comprehensive MRI-Based Framework.
abstract: Patient-specific musculoskeletal (MS) modeling can provide estimates of internal joint loading that canot be measured directly. However, limitations in automated segmentation due to data-scarce environments, morphing difficulty caused by anatomical variability, and functional non-alignment are major bottlenecks that hinder the practical application of modeling and reduce productivity in musculoskeletal research. To comprehensively address these practical issues, this study proposes and validates an integrated, automated modeling framework.. First, we automatically segmented the lower extremity bones of the 4 knee osteoarthritis patients using a multi-atlas-based segmentation algorithm. By integrating the segmented bone with motion capture and force plate data, a modeling pipeline including multi-stage morphing and functional alignment processes was implemented. Using the constructed customized model, the medial and lateral knee contact forces (FMC and FLC) were estimated during a single-leg step-up exercise, and these were compared and evaluated against the results based on manual segmentation. The contact forces estimated through the automated segmentation framework demonstrated high consistency with the manual results. The mean absolute error ranged from 0.04 ± 0.03 to 0.06 ± 0.03 BW for FMC, and from 0.06 ± 0.04 to 0.09 ± 0.07 BW for FLC, and the intraclass correlation coefficient demonstrated a high correlation of over 0.99 across all patients. This study demonstrated that the proposed automated pipeline provides a practical approach to address misalignment caused by anatomical variability, while generating joint load estimates equivalent to the manual approach. By addressing key methodological challenges, this study will bring patient-specific models closer to future clinical application, where they could help assess individual loading across different activities and inform treatment and rehabilitation strategies.

title: Whey Protein Isolate and Sappan Wood (Caesalpinia sappan L.) Infusion Modulates Muscle Damage and Inflammatory Biomarkers Following High-Intensity Interval Training in Sedentary Males.
abstract: High-intensity interval training (HIIT) can induce muscle damage and inflammatory responses, particularly in sedentary individuals. This study investigated the effects of whey protein isolate (WPI) combined with sappan wood (Caesalpinia sappan L.) infusion on muscle damage and inflammation following HIIT in sedentary male individuals. This double-blind randomized controlled trial included 39 sedentary males who were allocated to three groups: WPI-sappan (n=14), WPI (n=13), and control (n=12). The participants completed treadmill-based HIIT. The WPI-sappan group received 30 g of WPI combined with a sappan wood infusion prepared from 8.3 g of sappan wood powder. The WPI group received a WPI beverage, whereas the control group consumed a carbohydrate-only drink. All beverages contained 20 g of sucrose. Supplementation was administered immediately after exercise and daily for 4 d. Serum creatine kinase (CK), lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), skeletal troponin I (sTnI), interleukin (IL)-6, and IL-10 concentrations were measured at baseline and at 24, 48, and 96 h post-exercise. Data were analyzed using repeated-measures analysis of variance. CK concentrations increased significantly after HIIT across all groups, with significant effects of time, treatment, and the time×treatment interaction (P<0.05). The WPI-sappan group demonstrated lower CK concentrations during recovery than the control group. IL-6 concentrations were significantly lower in the WPI-sappan group (P=0.024), whereas IL-10 showed a significant time×treatment interaction (P=0.010). No significant treatment effects were observed for LDH or sTnI. WPI combined with sappan wood modulated selected biomarkers of muscle damage and inflammation following HIIT in sedentary males.

title: Silent mechanical adaptation: Passive mechanical properties of ankle-surrounding tissues in individuals with unilateral chronic ankle instability.
abstract: BackgroundChronic ankle instability (CAI) is a complex condition characterized by recurring sprains.ObjectiveOur study aimed to compare the tone, stiffness, and elasticity of the periarticular muscles, Achilles tendon (AT), and plantar fascia (PF) between the affected and non-affected limbs of individuals with unilateral CAI.MethodsThe cross-sectional study included 75 volunteers aged 18 to 45 years who had been diagnosed with CAI by a physician. Ankle instability was assessed using the Identification of Functional Ankle Instability (IdFAI). Passive mechanical properties (PMP), including frequency, stiffness, and logarithmic decrement, of the tibialis anterior (TA), peroneus longus (PL), medial and lateral gastrocnemius (MGC - LGC), AT, and PF were assessed bilaterally using the MyotonPRO. PMP were compared between sides, and relationships between IdFAI scores and PMP on the affected side were examined.ResultsThe mean age was 27.46 ± 4.23 years. Logarithmic decrement and stiffness values were higher on the affected side in the TA (p = 0.011, p = 0.027), PL (p = 0.017, p = 0.031), and PF (p = 0.020, p = 0.028) compared to the non-affected side. Logarithmic decrement was also higher in the MGC (p = 0.029) and LGC (p = 0.005). No significant difference in frequency was observed for any of these structures (p > 0.05). The AT showed no significant differences in frequency, stiffness, or logarithmic decrement between the affected and non-affected sides (p > 0.05).ConclusionsCAI is a multidimensional pathology characterized by deterioration of the PMP of the surrounding muscles and PF. These findings suggest that management of CAI should include interventions aimed at improving myofascial tissue elasticity in addition to neuromuscular rehabilitation.Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov, TRN: NCT06987435.

title: Differential Splinting After Zone II Flexor Tendon Repair: The Bidirectional Splint.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Zone II flexor tendon injuries remain challenging because of the risks of rupture, adhesions, and stiffness. Splint design may influence repair-site tension during early healing. We describe a novel bidirectional splint (B-splint) that applies differential tensioning and compare its outcomes with those of conventional dorsal blocking splinting.
METHODS: We retrospectively studied 59 patients (99 repaired tendons): 20 patients (31 tendons) treated with the B-splint after flexor digitorum profundus repair and 39 patients (68 tendons) treated with a dorsal blocking splint. The B-splint positions repaired digits in metacarpophalangeal flexion with interphalangeal extension while maintaining the noninjured digits in full extension. Functional outcomes were assessed using the modified Strickland score; tendon rupture and tenolysis were recorded. Categorical outcomes were compared using exact tests.
RESULTS: No ruptures occurred in the B-splint cohort versus 1 in the control cohort. Excellent outcomes occurred in 19 of 20 B-splint patients (95%) versus 30 of 39 controls (77%), favoring the B-splint without statistical significance (P = 0.141). Tenolysis was less frequent with the B-splint (5% versus 13%). No B-splint patients developed stiffness of the noninjured digits.
CONCLUSIONS: The B-splint was associated with favorable functional outcomes, no observed ruptures, and less tenolysis than conventional dorsal blocking splinting. It complements established rehabilitation strategies. Prospective studies are warranted to define its biomechanical and clinical role.

title: Bone Mineral Density in Physique-Focused and Non-Physique-Focused Female Collegiate Athletes: Associations With Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport Risk Factors.
abstract: Kolb, DE, Cipriano, NL, Moody, RA, Stephens, JA, Caldwell, LK, Lindley, MR, Ware, ME, and Deemer, SE. Bone mineral density in physique-focused and non-physique-focused female collegiate athletes: Associations with relative energy deficiency in sport risk factors. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-Bone mineral density (BMD) is a critical indicator of skeletal health and long-term injury risk in athletic populations. Female athletes are susceptible to changes in BMD because of sport-specific training demands, hormonal dysregulation, and energy availability. The present study aimed to compare BMD between physique-focused (PF; endurance, aesthetic, and weight-dependent sports) and non-physique-focused (NPF; ball, power, and skill-based sports) female collegiate athletes and assess risk factors associated with relative energy deficiency in sport (REDs) across both groups. Thirty-three female athletes were evaluated for BMD by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA), REDs risk using the Clinical Assessment Tool 2 (CAT2), anthropometric measurements, blood biomarkers, the Eating Disorder Examination Questionnaire (EDE-Q), and the Low Energy Availability in Females Questionnaire (LEAF-Q). Group differences were assessed using independent t-tests with significance set at p < 0.05. Physique-focused athletes demonstrated significantly lower DXA-derived z-scores at anteroposterior spine, right and left femur, and total body sites than NPF athletes (p < 0.001). There were no differences in leptin (p = 0.35), cortisol (p = 0.16), vitamin D (p = 0.29), LEAF-Q total score (p = 0.72), or global EDE-Q score (p = 0.10). No group differences in CAT2 REDs risk were observed; thus, subjects were combined: 19 athletes were classified as "green;" 12 were "yellow;" and 2 were "orange." Lower BMD in PF athletes supports the importance of early screening and targeted interventions to support bone health. These findings suggest sport type may influence skeletal outcomes independent of traditional REDs indicators, emphasizing the need for sport-specific assessment strategies.

title: Biomechanical comparison of parallel versus convergent screw fixation in Zadek osteotomy.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Zadek osteotomy is an increasingly utilized treatment for insertional Achilles tendinopathy (IAT), although an optimal fixation strategy remains unclear. This cadaveric study compared biomechanical outcomes of parallel and convergent screw fixation constructs following Zadek osteotomy. We hypothesized that convergent screw fixation would demonstrate greater stability.
METHODS: Five paired fresh-frozen human calcanei (10 specimens) underwent simulated Zadek osteotomy, receiving paired parallel and convergent screw fixations on contralateral limbs. Specimens were tested using a servohydraulic system and motion tracking. Axial loading was applied until construct failure. Primary biomechanical outcomes included construct stiffness, load at 2 mm displacement, ultimate load to failure, and displacement at failure. Comparisons were performed using paired t-tests. One specimen was excluded from final analysis due to premature failure.
RESULTS: No significant differences were observed between parallel and convergent constructs for any biomechanical outcome. Mean stiffness was 1415 ± 1337 N/mm for parallel constructs and 1360 ± 952 N/mm for convergent constructs (p = 0.96). Load at 2 mm displacement measured 707 ± 289 N and 892 ± 401 N, respectively (p = 0.54). Ultimate load to failure was 915 ± 266 N and 1065 ± 401 N, respectively (p = 0.55). Displacement at failure was similar between groups (p = 0.45). The combination shear-compression sliding at the osteotomy interface was the predominant mechanism of failure in both groups.
CONCLUSION: Parallel and convergent screw constructs demonstrated comparable initial fixation strengths following Zadek osteotomy, suggesting screw trajectory may have limited impact on construct stability. Further studies are needed to validate these findings clinically.

title: Long-Term Failure Rate of Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction Using All-Inside 4-Stranded Semitendinosus Autograft Is 20.5.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To evaluate outcomes (graft failure, Patient-Reported Outcome Measures, and knee stability) after primary isolated anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction using the all-inside technique with 4-stranded semitendinosus autograft fixed between 2 adjustable-loop cortical suspension devices, with a minimum follow-up of 10 years.
METHODS: Patients who underwent primary isolated ACL reconstruction using the all-inside 4-stranded semitendinosus between January 2011 and January 2013, with a minimum of 10-year follow-up, were included. Patients completed a standardized questionnaire and were offered a follow-up consultation. The questionnaire included the Tegner, ACL-Return to Sport after Injury, Subjective Knee Value, subjective International Knee Documentation Committee, and assessment of graft failure. Clinical evaluations and laxity measurements were conducted during follow-up consultations.
RESULTS: At a mean follow-up of 138 months (range: 122-159), 156 patients completed the questionnaire, and 111 were clinically evaluated. The mean age was 39.6 ± 9.7 years (range: 15-62). Graft failure occurred in 20.5% of cases (32/156). The mean decrease in Tegner was 1.03 ± 1.23 points, and 51% returned to their preinjury sport level. The median preoperative Tegner was 7.0 (interquartile range: 6.0-7.0). A higher preoperative Tegner was associated with an increased risk of graft failure (P = .016). Graft failure occurred in 23% of males and 16.6% of females (P = .461). Patients with grafts sized ≤8 mm (n = 85) had a failure rate of 17.5%, compared with 23.9% for grafts >8 mm (P = .441). The mean subjective International Knee Documentation Committee was 85.6 ± 13.5, Subjective Knee Value 79.2 ± 22.1, and ACL-Return to Sport after Injury 69.5 ± 26.5. Among patients without reported graft failure, 16.5% exhibited >3 mm differential anterior laxity, and 28% had a pivot-shift score ≥2.
CONCLUSIONS: At a minimum 10-year follow-up, primary isolated ACL reconstruction using an all-inside 4-stranded semitendinosus autograft showed a 20.5% graft failure rate, despite favorable patient-reported outcomes. A higher preoperative Tegner showed a trend toward increased graft failure.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV, retrospective case series.

title: Effects of Integrative Neuromuscular Training on Unilateral and Bilateral Lower-Extremity Sports Performance in Adolescent Female Sprinters: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Adolescent female athletes often exhibit more pronounced lower-limb asymmetry due to physiological differences, increasing injury risk. Despite documented efficacy in team sports for injury mitigation and performance enhancement, integrative neuromuscular training (INT) effects on unilateral and bilateral lower-limb capabilities in trained adolescent female sprinters remain undetermined.
HYPOTHESIS: We hypothesized that an 8-week INT program would significantly improve unilateral and bilateral lower-extremity performance measures in adolescent female sprinters compared with traditional sprint-specific training.
STUDY DESIGN: Randomized controlled trial.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 1.
METHODS: Twenty-four national second-level adolescent female sprinters (aged 16-18 years) were randomly assigned to an 8-week INT group (n = 12) or a control group (CON, n = 12) that continued traditional sprint-specific training. Measurements obtained before and after the intervention included the hop test, star excursion balance test (SEBT), 3-repetition maximum (3RM) unilateral and bilateral back squat, 100-m run, standing long jump (SLJ), and limb symmetry index (LSI).
RESULTS: After the intervention, the INT group outperformed the CON group on the nondominant side in all hop tests (P < 0.001; ηp² = 0.74-0.88), six directions of the SEBT (P < 0.001; ηp² = 0.44-0.88), and the 3RM unilateral back squat (P < 0.01; ηp² = 0.65). On the dominant side, the INT group also outperformed the CON group in the single hop for distance (P < 0.001; ηp² = 0.80) and three directions of the SEBT (P < 0.01; ηp² = 0.38-0.84). In addition, the INT group showed significantly greater improvements than the CON group in the LSI from unilateral tests (all P < 0.01; ηp² = 0.26-0.88), as well as in the 100-m run and SLJ (P < 0.001; ηp² = 0.61-0.69).
CONCLUSION: The 8-week INT program was associated with improvements in dynamic balance, explosive power, and limb symmetry in adolescent female sprinters, with greater benefits observed on the nondominant side.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: INT is an effective training modality for improving lower-limb performance and mitigating asymmetry in adolescent female sprinters.

title: Early sub-maximal quadriceps motor unit firing characteristics and six-month knee extensor strength after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction: a prospective longitudinal study.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To determine whether quadriceps motor unit firing rates measured pre-operatively and during the first three months after anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction are associated with isometric knee extensor strength at six months, and to explore the relationship between motor unit action potential (MUAP) amplitude and firing rate.
METHODS: Twenty-seven participants (15 female) underwent surface electromyography of vastus medialis and vastus lateralis during sub-maximal isometric knee extension from pre-operation to three months post-reconstruction. Six-month knee extensor MVC force was modelled using Bayesian regression and interpreted using a region of practical equivalence (ROPE; ±15 N). A secondary hierarchical analysis examined MUAP amplitude and firing rate.
RESULTS: Motor unit firing rate was not consistently associated with six-month knee extensor strength across time points and limbs. In the ACL reconstructed limb at two weeks, a 1-SD greater mean firing rate was associated with 45.8 N greater six-month strength (95% credible interval [CrI] - 18.5 to 114.6 N). Six-month strength was greater in the contralateral limb (β = 198.4 N, 95% CrI 171.6 to 225.1 N), in males (β = 184.3 N, 95% CrI 32.0 to 325.1 N), and with greater body mass (β = 119.9 N per 1-SD, 95% CrI 33.4 to 207.2 N). Greater relative MUAP amplitude was associated with lower firing rate (-3.7 Hz per 1-SD, 95% CrI -3.8 to -3.6 Hz).
CONCLUSIONS: Sub-maximal quadriceps motor unit firing rate was not consistently associated with later knee extensor strength, although a stronger positive association was suggested in the reconstructed limb at two weeks. Firing rate was strongly related to relative MUAP amplitude, and its predictive value for later strength appears limited.

title: Dose-dependent effects of sodium bicarbonate supplementation combined with sprint interval training on performance adaptations in basketball players: a randomized placebo-controlled trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Sprint interval training (SIT) effectively improves physical performance in team-sport athletes, while sodium bicarbonate (Sb) supplementation may enhance training adaptations. However, the dose-dependent effects of Sb during SIT remain unclear in basketball players. Therefore, this study examined the effects of two Sb doses combined with SIT on physical performance adaptations in basketball players.
METHODS: Forty trained male basketball players (age: 21.6 ± 2.0 years, height: 185.4 ± 3.5 cm, body mass: 84.1 ± 4.4 kg) were recruited and randomly assigned to four groups: SIT + 0.3 g·kg-1 Sb (n = 10), SIT + 0.45 g·kg-1 Sb (n = 10), SIT + placebo (PL) (n = 10), and control (CON) (n = 10). The intervention lasted four weeks during the preparatory phase of the season. Participants in the training groups performed SIT three times per week in addition to their regular basketball training. The SIT protocol consisted of four sets of ten 5-second maximal sprints, with 20 seconds of active recovery between repetitions and 2 minutes of rest between sets. All 40 enrolled participants successfully completed the 4-week intervention, resulting in a 0% dropout rate. Performance assessments conducted before and after the intervention included countermovement vertical jump (CMVJ), standing long jump (SLJ), 20 m sprint, Illinois change-of-direction speed (CODS), Yo-Yo Intermittent Recovery Test Level 1 (Yo-Yo IR1), and Wingate anaerobic power (peak power output [PPO] and mean power output [MPO]).
RESULTS: All training groups showed significant improvements in physical performance variables over time (p < 0.05). Significant group by time interaction effects were observed for all performance variables (p ≤ 0.001), indicating that the SIT groups showed more gains compared with the CON group. Both Sb supplementation groups demonstrated greater improvements than the SIT + PL group in CMVJ, SLJ, sprint performance, CODS, Yo-Yo IR1 distance, PPO, and MPO (p < 0.05). Furthermore, the SIT + 0.45 g·kg-1 Sb group exhibited significantly greater performance enhancements than the SIT + 0.3 g·kg-1 Sb group across all measured variables.
CONCLUSION: Four weeks of SIT improved performance in trained basketball players, with Sb supplementation providing additional dose-dependent benefits (0.45 > 0.3 g⋅kg-1). While the higher dose yielded superior adaptations, its practical application should be balanced against potential gastrointestinal discomfort and individual tolerance to ensure long-term athlete compliance.

title: Effects of Fatigue on Peak and Angle-Specific Hamstring-to-Quadriceps Ratios in Collegiate Women Lacrosse Athletes.
abstract: Background: Hamstring strains and anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tears commonly occur in court and field sport athletes, with prevalence being higher in females. The likelihood of such injuries has been related to the hamstring-to-quadriceps (H:Q) strength ratio. Such a ratio can be affected by fatigue, to which athletes are frequently exposed. The aim of the current study was to investigate effects of fatigue on peak torque and angle-specific functional H:Q ratios at different angular velocities, as well as the association between resting functional H:Q ratios and those obtained following fatigue. Methods: A total of 18 collegiate women lacrosse players executed maximal knee concentric and eccentric contractions at angular velocities of 60, 180, and 240°/s following a supervised fatigue protocol. The isokinetic testing was then replicated. Results: There was a significant difference in functional peak torque H:Q ratios (p = 0.021-0.041) and ratios at 60 (p = 0.013-0.044), but not 20 degrees of knee flexion before and after fatigue at all three angular velocities. No main effects of angular velocity or ratio type were observed on H:Q ratio difference. The relationship between resting and fatigued functional H:Q ratios ranged from moderate to strong across all three angular velocities. Conclusions: Fatigue was associated with reductions in functional H:Q ratios, indicating altered knee flexor-extensor strength balance under fatigued conditions. In time-constrained settings, baseline functional H:Q ratio may provide practitioners with useful preliminary information regarding an athlete's potential susceptibility to lower-limb injury after fatigue.

title: Tracking Recovery After TKA with Instrumented Timed Up and Go: Spatiotemporal, Rotational, and Strength Adaptations over Six Months.
abstract: Knee osteoarthritis (KOA) is a leading cause of disability, and total knee arthroplasty (TKA) improves pain and functional mobility, although gait impairments may persist postoperatively. This study investigated longitudinal changes in patient-reported outcomes, muscle strength, and gait performance using an instrumented Timed Up and Go (iTUG) test with wearable inertial measurement units (IMUs). Twenty-two patients with end-stage KOA were assessed preoperatively and at 3, 12, and 24 weeks postoperatively. The Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score five-subscale composite (KOOS5) showed a significant overall change over time (p < 0.001), while isometric muscle strength showed significant overall changes across all tested muscle groups (p ≤ 0.008), with mean values demonstrating an initial postoperative decline followed by subsequent increases. Total TUG duration showed a significant overall time effect (p = 0.023), with significant reductions observed in the forward and return gait phases (p = 0.012 and p = 0.001, respectively). End-turning maximum rotational speed and sit-to-stand vertical acceleration showed significant overall time effects (p = 0.012 and p = 0.024, respectively), whereas the remaining parameters did not reach statistical significance. These findings indicate that recovery following TKA is multidimensional, with significant changes in patient-reported outcomes, muscle strength, and functional mobility. iTUG analysis identified phase-specific changes, while several turning and transitional parameters did not show significant longitudinal changes, supporting the use of targeted rehabilitation strategies focusing on dynamic stability and movement control.

title: All-Suture Fixation for Acute Turf Toe Injuries.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Turf toe is a hallux metatarsophalangeal joint (MTPJ) injury caused by hyperextension of the great toe with axial loading1,2. High-grade injuries may threaten return to sport and require surgery3,4. Here, we describe a capsular reconstruction of the great toe MTPJ with all-knotless suture anchors and suture tape augmentation for turf toe injuries, in isolation or in combination with a traumatic bunion, designed to reduce suture burden, minimize soft-tissue irritation, and facilitate recovery.
DESCRIPTION: The procedure begins with the patient supine. A direct medial approach to the hallux MTPJ is performed. Both the medial base of the proximal phalanx and the medial eminence of the metatarsal head are drilled at isometric points, and augmentation with suture tape is then performed. Isometric drill holes are placed in the medial proximal phalanx base and metatarsal head for suture tape augmentation. A knotless suture anchor is placed approximately 3 mm proximal to the articular margin of the metatarsal head, repairing the medial capsule in a horizontal mattress fashion. An additional knotless anchor is placed at the plantar plate insertion, and the suture is passed through the tibial sesamoid sling and tensioned with the toe in 20° of plantar flexion. Suture tape is secured into the proximal phalanx with an interference screw, then passed through the deep capsule into the metatarsal head, followed by the placement of an additional interference screw into the metatarsal head. The anchor is inserted into the plantar-medial proximal phalanx at the flexor hallucis brevis insertion. The toe is flexed during tensioning, then adjusted per clinical examination and the sesamoid location beneath the metatarsal head. Knotless fixation permits incremental tensioning with intraoperative assessment of motion. Final tensioning is performed with the toe in neutral to correct deformity without overconstraint, preserving range of motion.
ALTERNATIVES: Nonoperative alternatives include rest, ice, compression and elevation; anti-inflammatory drugs; activity modification; and brief immobilization5,6. Operative alternatives include primary capsuloligamentous complex repair with nonabsorbable sutures, plantar plate advancement with bone tunnels or suture anchors if primary repair is not feasible, and concomitant procedures such as sesamoidectomy and bunionectomy based on the injury pattern2,7,8.
RATIONALE: This technique is intended for high-grade turf toe injuries with capsuloligamentous disruption, sesamoid complex insufficiency, and MTPJ instability. Nonoperative treatment may be appropriate in cases of low-grade injury; however, persistent pain, instability, or loss of push-off strength following nonoperative treatment would indicate a higher-grade injury. Compared with isolated repair or plantar plate advancement alone, this technique restores both static and dynamic stabilizers of the hallux MTPJ while addressing associated angular deformity. Suture tape augmentation resists recurrent hyperextension and valgus forces while allowing controlled physiologic motion. Knotless, low-profile suture anchors minimize bulk and hardware prominence in a region with limited soft-tissue coverage and bone stock. This construct offers a robust reconstruction option for athletes requiring predictable restoration of stability and reliable return to sport.
EXPECTED OUTCOMES: Operative treatment of high-grade turf toe injuries has been shown to result in reliable pain relief, restored stability, and high rates of return to sport8. Previous studies have suggested improved function and earlier return to play compared with prolonged nonoperative treatment in appropriate patients6,7. Knotless suture anchors reduce implant prominence and eliminate knot-related irritation, while the small insertional diameter of the suture anchors preserves bone stock in the metatarsal head and proximal phalanx. This construct provides immediate stability while allowing controlled motion, facilitating rehabilitation, and reducing postoperative stiffness. Athletes typically return to unrestricted activity within 6 to 9 months, aided by the suture tape augmentation allowing earlier movement through the range of motion. This augmentation reduces the need for long-term spica splinting and bracing and reduces the risk of recurrence.
IMPORTANT TIPS: The small anchor diameter and use of suture tape allow easy access without hardware burden.○ Suture choice depends on surgeon preference regarding construct stiffness and on the tissue quality and risk of irritation. We believe that suture tape lays flatter and, if required, knots are smaller.Avoid suture twisting or kinking, which can prematurely lock anchors, compromising fixation.○ After the anchor is placed, we keep the suture tape secured out of the field as we prepare the capsule with absorbable suture. As we load the second anchor, we maintain tension on the tape to prevent twisting.Overtightening the MTPJ capsule may lead to altered biomechanics.
ACRONYMS AND ABBREVIATIONS: RICE = rest, ice, compression, elevationMRI = magnetic resonance imagingBID = twice daily.

title: Bony Anatomy, Soft-Tissue Adaptations and Neuromuscular Risk Factors of Shoulder Injury in Handball Players: A Narrative Review.
abstract: Handball is a high-intensity contact sport that imposes significant mechanical stress on the shoulder joint through repetitive, high-velocity overhead throwing, predisposing athletes to a wide spectrum of shoulder injuries. This narrative review examines the factors associated with shoulder injuries in handball players, highlighting underlying structural, adaptive and functional mechanisms across male and female athletes. A literature search of PubMed/MEDLINE was conducted to synthesize current evidence on bony anatomy, soft tissue adaptations and neuromuscular characteristics in handball cohorts. Factors associated with shoulder injury or symptoms can be broadly categorized into three conceptual domains: (i) bony anatomy and structural features, (ii) soft tissue adaptations and (iii) dynamic functional and neuromuscular factors. Bony factors include reduced acromiohumeral distance, increased humeral retrotorsion as a sport-specific skeletal adaptation and variations in glenoid morphology that may influence glenohumeral stability. Soft tissue adaptations include posterior capsular tightness, anterior capsular laxity and alterations in shoulder range of motion, particularly glenohumeral internal rotation deficit (GIRD) accompanied by external rotation gain (ERG), which may influence glenohumeral kinematics and potentially contribute to shoulder symptoms or overuse conditions. Beyond these structural features, dynamic functional factors, including shoulder rotator muscle strength imbalances, impaired scapular control and training-load management, play a central role in injury development. Therefore, a comprehensive assessment encompassing anatomical correlates, soft tissue characteristics and functional/neuromuscular characteristics may support the development of targeted injury-prevention and rehabilitation strategies in handball players.

title: Sleep Characteristics of Elite Female Soccer Players Competing in the National Women's Soccer League Across a Competitive Season.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Sleep supports recovery and readiness in professional sport, yet season-long objective data in women's professional soccer are limited. This study aimed to provide a longitudinal, objective description of sleep across a competitive season and to compare sleep characteristics between preseason and in-season phases.
METHODS: Twenty-seven professional athletes were monitored from January to November 2024 using a finger-worn wearable. Nightly total sleep time (TST), sleep efficiency, sleep onset latency (SOL), and sleep stage durations were extracted. Preseason versus in-season differences were examined using linear mixed-effects models and reported as estimated marginal mean differences with 95% CIs.
RESULTS: During the in-season, TST averaged 7.8 (1.2) hours (median: 7.9 h), sleep efficiency 89.1% (5.4%), and SOL 15.6 (12.6) minutes. Mean sleep stage durations were 262.8 (52.8) minutes (light), 96.6 (31.8) minutes (deep), and 106.8 (34.2) minutes (Rapid Eye Movement). Notable night-to-night variability was observed, particularly for TST (within-player coefficients of variation: 10%-18%) and SOL (50%-114%). Compared with preseason, in-season sleep was characterized by lower REM sleep (-4.8 min, 95% CI -6.9 to -2.8; P < .001), reduced sleep efficiency (-0.37%, 95% CI -0.71 to -0.02; P = .036), and shorter SOL (-1.1 min, 95% CI -2.0 to -0.2; P = .020). TST did not differ between phases (P = .287), and deep and light sleep remained unchanged. Effect sizes were small (Cohen d ≤ 0.15).
CONCLUSIONS: Group averages of sleep parameters might mask individual and seasonal changes in sleep, highlighting the need for longitudinal, athlete-specific monitoring to guide proactive sleep monitoring strategies.

title: Sleep Quality and Sleep Timing in Adolescent Gymnasts: A Cross-Sectional Study.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Given the limited pediatric-specific evidence in this area, we aimed to examine the association between federated-level gymnastics participation and sleep quality and sleep timing in adolescents. The global Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) score was defined as the primary outcome, sleep-timing measures as secondary outcomes, and individual PSQI component analyses as exploratory.
METHODS: This observational, cross-sectional comparative study included adolescents aged 12 to 16 years participating in federated gymnastics and controls who did not participate in federated sports. Demographic variables included age, sex, and parental educational level, while training-related variables included weekly training duration, number of training sessions, and training schedule. Sleep quality was assessed using the PSQI, and bedtime, wake-up time, sleep duration, and sleep latency were derived from the corresponding PSQI items. Multiple linear regression models included age, sex, maternal educational level, and paternal educational level as covariates.
RESULTS: The study included 60 gymnasts and 37 controls, with baseline differences in age, sex distribution, and parental educational level between groups. Gymnasts trained a median of 12.0 hours/week (Q1-Q3: 8.25 to 20.0) over five sessions/week (Q1-Q3: 4 to 6), with a median training-session end time of 20:30 (range: 18:00 to 22:00). In adjusted analyses, gymnast status was associated with later bedtime (B=0.392 hours, 95% CI 0.043 to 0.740, p=0.028), whereas no statistically significant association was observed between study group and global PSQI score (B=0.311, 95% CI -0.720 to 1.343, p=0.550). Increasing age was associated with later bedtime (B=0.231 hours, p=0.004) and shorter sleep duration (B=-0.398 hours, 95% CI -0.560 to -0.236, p<0.001). Among gymnasts, training-session end time was not associated with global PSQI score (B=0.141, 95% CI -0.344 to 0.625, p=0.563; R²=0.006). Overall, 19/97 participants (19.6%) met the conventional PSQI >5 threshold for poor sleep quality, although an optimal adolescent-specific clinical cutoff has not been definitively established.
CONCLUSION: No statistically significant difference in adjusted global PSQI score was detected between federated adolescent gymnasts and controls. Gymnast status was associated with later bedtime. Approximately one in five participants met the conventional PSQI >5 threshold for poor sleep quality. Given the cross-sectional design, these findings should be interpreted as associations, and larger longitudinal studies incorporating objective sleep measures are warranted.

title: Greater weapon-side supraspinatus tendon thickness in elite national-team fencers: an exploratory cross-sectional ultrasound study.
abstract: Fencing exposes the weapon arm to repetitive loading that differs from conventional overhead sports, yet shoulder morphology in elite fencers is poorly described. We compared supraspinatus tendon thickness, resting acromiohumeral distance (AHD), and occupation ratio between shoulders in 15 elite national-team fencers without current shoulder pain during daily life or competition. Bilateral ultrasonography measured tendon thickness at 5 and 10 mm lateral to the biceps tendon in the modified Crass position. Mean tendon thickness was greater on the weapon side (5.37 ± 0.89 vs 4.67 ± 0.96 mm; mean difference, 0.70 mm; 95% CI, 0.30 to 1.11; p = 0.002), with the difference most evident at 5 mm. No statistically significant between-side difference in resting AHD was detected (p = 0.085), whereas occupation ratio was higher on the weapon side (p = 0.013). Our findings suggest that fencers' shoulders can differ in structure even when neither side is painful. This is worth remembering when the opposite shoulder is used as an ultrasound reference, although the cause and clinical relevance of the difference are not yet known.

title: Eating Behavior, Body Appreciation, and Sleep Quality in Italian Blind Baseball Athletes: A Cross-Sectional Exploratory Survey.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Visual impairment is associated with poor sleep quality, psychological distress, and unhealthy lifestyle behaviors. Adapted sports, such as blind baseball (BXC), may help promote healthy lifestyles and overall well-being. However, evidence regarding eating behavior, sleep quality, body appreciation, and lifestyle habits among regular BXC players remains scarce. This cross-sectional study provides an exploratory multidimensional characterization of these domains in competitive Italian BXC athletes according to sport participation and visual impairment characteristics, comparing findings descriptively with normative data from the Italian general population. Methods: Fifty-three competitive Italian BXC players (mean age 39.3 ± 13.1 years; representing a response rate of 49.1% of the national league) completed an anonymous online survey assessing eating behavior (Adult Eating Behavior Questionnaire, AEBQ), body appreciation (Body Appreciation Scale-2, BAS-2), sleep quality (Brief Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, B-PSQI), and lifestyle habits. Group differences were assessed using chi-square tests for categorical variables and Mann-Whitney U tests for continuous variables, reporting medians, interquartile ranges, effect sizes (rank-biserial r), and 95% confidence intervals. Results: BXC athletes demonstrated BMI, sleep quality, eating behavior, and body appreciation profiles comparable to those of the Italian general population. BAS-2 scores were high (3.7-3.8), while B-PSQI scores (4.0-5.6) and the proportion of poor sleepers (~40%) remained within normative ranges despite visual impairment. Eating behavior showed no significant dysregulation. However, in exploratory subgroup analyses, multisport athletes displayed lower Satiety Responsiveness than BXC-only athletes (2.30 ± 0.79 vs. 2.78 ± 0.71; p = 0.02), poorer sleep quality (B-PSQI: 6.05 ± 3.12 vs. 4.70 ± 3.73; p = 0.05), and a higher prevalence of poor sleep (55.0% vs. 30.3%). Athletes with acquired visual impairment showed higher Emotional Overeating and Emotional Undereating scores than those with congenital impairment, although these differences did not reach statistical significance. Conclusions: BXC athletes displayed an overall favorable lifestyle profile. Though the cross-sectional design prevents causal inferences, these exploratory findings indicate that participation in BXC is compatible with healthy lifestyle habits and positive body appreciation, hence supporting adapted team sports as an inclusive framework for multidimensional health promotion. Future studies using objective physiological assessments and longitudinal designs are needed to clarify dose-response relationships and long-term health outcomes.
