title: Use of Botanical Ingredients Relevant to Premenstrual Symptoms and Dysmenorrhea Among Elite Female Athletes: Evidence from Doping Control Forms.
abstract:
BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: Premenstrual syndrome (PMS) and dysmenorrhea can impair training performance in female athletes. Botanical ingredients are commonly used to manage these conditions in the general population, but it is unknown whether elite female athletes do so. This study aimed to identify botanical ingredients evaluated in studies for PMS and dysmenorrhea and determine whether elite female athletes declared them on Doping Control Forms (DCFs).
METHODS: A narrative literature review was conducted to identify botanical ingredients evaluated in studies for PMS and dysmenorrhea. Then, DCFs completed during routine anti-doping testing among elite athletes in Poland (2018-2023) were analyzed for declarations of these ingredients, both directly and as components of multi-ingredient products. The proportion of DCFs containing these ingredients was compared between female (n = 4451 DCFs) and male athletes (n = 9068 DCFs; reference) using chi-squared tests.
RESULTS: The review identified 8 and 21 botanical ingredients with evidence for PMS and dysmenorrhea, respectively; of which 9 were detected in DCFs. The most commonly declared ingredients among female athletes were ginger and turmeric/curcuminoid (1.75% and 1.26%, respectively, both studied for PMS and dysmenorrhea). Chasteberry, on the other hand, with the most extensive, albeit low-confidence evidence, for PMS, was rarely declared (0.22%). Direct declaration of ginkgo, valerian, evening primrose oil, and chasteberry was significantly more common among female than male athletes (0.22% vs. 0.02%, 0.36% vs. 0.03%, 0.47% vs. 0.03%, 0.22% vs. 0.02%; adjusted p < 0.05).
CONCLUSIONS: Declarations of botanical ingredients studied for PMS and dysmenorrhea were infrequent on DCFs completed by female athletes. Because DCFs do not record the reason for use, these data cannot establish whether declarations reflected treatment of menstrual symptoms; studies assessing indication, symptom status and motivation are needed.

title: Five-Year Outcomes and Return to Sport After Arthroscopic Bankart Repair in Young Patients With Minimal (<10%) or No Glenoid Bone Loss.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Arthroscopic Bankart repair is commonly used to address anterior instability in adolescents and young adults with no or minimal bone loss. However, failure rates remain high, particularly in high-risk populations.
PURPOSE/HYPOTHESIS: The purpose of this study was to evaluate clinical outcomes, return-to-sport (RTS) rates, and predictors of failure after arthroscopic Bankart repair in patients ≤24 years of age with minimal glenoid bone loss. It was hypothesized that patients would demonstrate favorable outcomes, low recurrence rates, and high RTS rates, and smaller distance-to-dislocation (DTD) measurements, and contact sports participation would be associated with failure.
STUDY DESIGN: Case series; Level of evidence, 4.
METHODS: The data of patients with anterior shoulder instability and minimal bone loss (<10%) who underwent primary arthroscopic Bankart repair between 2006 and 2020 were retrospectively analyzed. Remplissage was not performed. Data collected included preoperative instability events, patient-reported outcome measures, satisfaction, radiographic measurements (glenoid bone loss, glenoid track, and DTD), and RTS outcomes. Failure was defined as re-dislocation or recurrent instability requiring surgery.
RESULTS: A total of 130 patients were evaluated; 18 were excluded, leaving 112. Of these, 96 patients (85.7%) were available for the final follow-up (mean age, 19.9 ± 3.1 years; mean follow-up, 68.4 ± 42.7 months). All clinical outcomes improved significantly (P < .05) except for the 12-Item Short Form Health Survey Mental Component Summary score. The median satisfaction score was 9 (IQR, 8-10). Participation in contact sports was associated with failure, while other risk factors were not. RTS was achieved by 96.1% of patients; however, only 57.1% returned to their preinjury level. Fewer preoperative dislocation events were associated with successful return to full activity (P = .04). The recurrence rate was 33.3%, and revision surgery was required in 19 patients (19.8%).
CONCLUSION: Arthroscopic Bankart repair was associated with high rates of recurrence and revision surgery in a series of patients ≤24 years of age without glenoid bone loss. In those who did not require revision surgery, clinical outcomes and RTS rates were high. Contact sports participation was associated with failure. A greater number of preoperative instability events negatively influence RTS outcomes. Arthroscopic Bankart repair in this population is safe and has a low complication rate, but the failure rate remains considerable.

title: Menstrual Cycle Phase-Dependent Lower Extremity Loading Patterns in Adolescent Female Athletes: Implications for Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury Risk.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Physically active females experience substantially higher anterior cruciate ligament injury rates than males, and postmenarche adolescent females commonly demonstrate high-risk mechanics. However, whether mechanics fluctuate across the menstrual cycle remains poorly understood in adolescent female athletes. The aim of this study was to examine differences in lower extremity kinematics and kinetics across two menstrual cycle phases (menstruation and mid-luteal) in postmenarchal adolescent female athletes during a dynamic change-of-direction task. It was hypothesized that biomechanical contributors to dynamic knee valgus would differ between phases.
METHODS: A controlled laboratory study was conducted. Thirty healthy postmenarchal adolescent female athletes (aged 13-17 years) were tested during menstruation (verified by self-reported active bleeding) and mid-luteal phase (scheduled via calendar-based day counting). Kinematics and kinetics were collected using 3-dimensional motion capture and force plates while participants performed a 45° run-cut task. Peak pelvis, hip, and knee angles and hip and knee moments were extracted during the loading phase for each limb. Linear mixed-effects models tested effects of phase and limb dominance (α = 0.05).
RESULTS: Participants were aged 15.6 ± 0.9 years, had a height of 168.8 ± 6.2 cm, and weighed 61.2 ± 7.0 kg, and a majority played soccer (70.0%). Compared with menstruation, the mid-luteal phase demonstrated greater peak anterior pelvic tilt (P = .018) and pelvic rise (P = .038), along with reduced peak knee flexion (P = .009). During menstruation, athletes exhibited greater hip abduction moment (P = .037), hip internal rotation moment (P = .043), knee valgus moment (P = .012), and knee external rotation moment (P = .007). Limb dominance effects were observed for pelvic rise (P < .001) and hip internal rotation moment (P = .047).
CONCLUSIONS: Biomechanical contributors linked to dynamic knee valgus differed by menstrual cycle phase in adolescent female athletes during a change-of-direction task. Menstruation was associated with greater coronal- and transverse-plane hip and knee loading, whereas mid-luteal phase was associated with reduced knee flexion and greater pelvic instability. Cycle-synced injury prevention strategies that are individualized and evidence-based may enhance lower extremity stability when knee control appears most challenged. However, while cycle-synced training may not be feasible in all settings, awareness of phase-related vulnerability may inform screening and load management.
KEY CONCEPTS: (1)Menstrual cycle phase may contribute to variability in lower extremity biomechanics during change-of-direction tasks in adolescent female athletes.(2)Biomechanical risk factors associated with dynamic knee valgus may differ between menstruation and mid-luteal phases.(3)Consideration of menstrual cycle phase may improve interpretation of biomechanical screening and performance testing.(4)Individualized injury prevention strategies may benefit from awareness of phase-related biomechanical changes.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: III.

title: An Intensified Training Period Reduces REM Sleep but this Decline Can Be Mitigated by Ketone Ester Supplementation.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: We previously showed that a strenuous training day disrupts sleep efficiency and REM sleep, and that these disturbances can be counteracted by ketone monoester (R)-3-hydroxybutyl-(R)-3-hydroxybutyrate (KE) supplementation. However, the impact of prolonged intensified training on sleep quality, as well as the potential modulating effect of KE are unknown.
METHODS: We performed a double-blind study in which twenty-four trained male athletes completed a 7-week training program with a gradual increase in training load while receiving either 25g of a control drink (CON, n=12) or 25g of KE (n=12) after each training session and 30 minutes before sleep. At the start (PRE), week 3 (MID), and the end (POST) of the training program, we evaluated sleep using polysomnography, and perceived stress/recovery balance using the REST-Q questionnaire. Timing, duration, and relative intensity of exercise on each testing day were identical.
RESULTS: The progressive increase in training load induced a decrease in the perceived stress-recovery state in both groups (PRE: 73±21 vs. POST: 40±37, p<0.001, Hedges' g = 1.097). From PRE to MID, sleep efficiency improved by 3% in both groups (p=0.003, Hedges' g = 0.663) while wakefulness after sleep onset reduced by 2% (p=0.031, Hedges' g = 0.716). However, from PRE to POST, total REM sleep decreased by 2% in CON but increased by 3% in KE (p=0.002, for KE vs. CON, Hedges' g = 0.939). Perceived sleep quality did not differ between groups throughout the intervention.
CONCLUSIONS: Our data indicate that KE supplementation did not enhance the beneficial effect of an initial increase in training load on sleep but prevented the decline in REM sleep upon a further training load increment.

title: Validity of triaxial accelerometer for estimating total energy expenditure in elite female university athletes: a doubly labeled water study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Accurate estimation of total energy expenditure (TEE) in athletes is essential for determining energy requirements to support training, recovery, and performance. Basal metabolic rate (BMR) is one of the key components associated with the accuracy of TEE estimation. However, few studies have evaluated the accuracy of BMR and TEE estimation methods in athletic populations.
OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to examine the validity of the Cunningham equation for BMR estimation and the accelerometer-based method (ACCTRI) for TEE estimation in elite female university runners, using the doubly labeled water (DLW) method as the reference criterion.
METHODS: We analyzed data from 16 elite female university runners (mean age 20 ± 1 years). We assessed: (1) the association and agreement between BMR estimated using the Cunningham equation and BMR measured by indirect calorimetry, and (2) the association and agreement between TEE estimated using the ACCTRI method and TEE measured using the DLW method.
RESULTS: Correlational analysis revealed significant, positive, and strong associations between estimated and measured BMR (r = 0.728, P = 0.001) and between estimated and measured TEE (r = 0.828, P = 0.001). Bland-Altman analyses showed good agreement between estimated and measured BMR (bias, ~1.6%). The mean TEE difference between two method was 416 ± 242 kcal/day.
CONCLUSIONS: The Cunningham equation provides reasonably accurate estimates of BMR. ACCTRI overestimated TEE by approximately 12% compared to DLW, thus support staff should consider this when supporting female runners.

title: Structured Physiotherapy Improves Functional Outcomes in Acromegalic Arthropathy After Biochemical Remission: A Prospective Controlled Study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Musculoskeletal symptoms frequently persist in acromegaly despite biochemical remission, yet the impact of structured physiotherapy on pain, stiffness, and function remains poorly defined.
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the effects of a standardized knee-focused physiotherapy program in controlled acromegaly and to identify clinical predictors of treatment responsiveness.
METHODS: Thirteen patients with acromegaly in remission and 13 age-, gender-, and BMI-matched individuals with primary knee osteoarthritis completed a 15-session physiotherapy program. Outcomes were assessed pre- and post-intervention using the Brief Pain Inventory (BPI) and WOMAC. Minimal clinically significant difference (MCID) thresholds (≥2 for BPI, ≥10 for WOMAC) determined meaningful improvement. Correlation analyses examined associations between clinical variables and Δ scores.
RESULTS: Acromegaly patients showed significant improvements in all BPI and WOMAC domains (p<0.001). MCID was achieved by 85% for BPI and 100% for WOMAC Total. Pain and function improved most, whereas stiffness showed limited responsiveness. Compared with osteoarthritis controls, acromegaly patients demonstrated smaller Δ changes; baseline-adjusted analyses (ANCOVA) indicated that this attenuated response was largely explained by greater baseline severity in the control group, whereas the persistently greater stiffness in acromegaly remained significant even after adjustment. BMI correlated positively with improvements in BPI Total (r = 0.63) and BPI Pain Severity (r = 0.69), while adenoma size correlated negatively with both measures (r = -0.57 and -0.60). BMI showed a negative association with WOMAC Total improvement (r = -0.59). Stiffness changes were strongly negatively correlated with pretreatment IGF-1 (r = -0.77).
CONCLUSION: Structured physiotherapy yields clinically meaningful improvements in pain and function in acromegaly, while stiffness appears less reversible and more structurally driven. Early musculoskeletal assessment and physiotherapy integration may enhance long-term management.

title: Talking about menstruation in professional women's sport: gendered communication between athletes, coaches and team-mates.
abstract: Communication about menstruation remains uneven within sporting environments despite growing recognition of the importance of menstrual health for athletes. This article investigates how female athletes communicate about menstruation and how gendered hierarchies shape these interactions. The analysis is based on responses to an online questionnaire completed by Polish professional athletes (N = 253). The findings indicate that menstruation is seldom discussed between athletes and coaches, with participants identifying social and institutional barriers, including menstrual taboo and the predominance of male coaches. In contrast, athletes reported discussing menstruation more openly with female team-mates, where such conversations often facilitated mutual support and the sharing of experiential knowledge about menstrual health. These interactions suggest that women's teams can function as 'counterspaces' where menstrual experiences can be acknowledged and normalised in ways largely absent from coach-athlete relationships. Findings highlight the importance of creating environments in which menstrual health can be openly discussed, as limited communication about menstruation may restrict athletes' access to information, support, and health-related guidance. By examining menstruation as a topic of health-related communication, the study contributes to scholarship on gender, embodiment and menstrual health, highlighting how institutional hierarchies shape the visibility and discussion of bodily processes across different social contexts.

title: Acute neurotrophic responses to a single bout of blood flow restriction and eccentric overload exercise in healthy older men.
abstract: Blood flow restriction training (BFRT) combines substantial metabolic stress with low mechanical loading, but its neurotrophic effects remain unclear. This study investigated the acute effects of BFRT and eccentric overload exercise (EOE) on neurotrophic biomarkers in healthy older men. Sixty-three healthy older men (60-78 years) were randomized to BFRT, EOE, or a non-exercising control group. Neurotrophic, metabolic, endothelial, and muscle damage biomarkers were measured before and after exercise. Responses were analyzed using repeated-measures ANOVA, Bonferroni-adjusted post hoc comparisons, and correlations. Significant time × group interactions were observed for plasma BDNF (p = 0.017, ηp2 = 0.151) and IL-6 (p = 0.001, ηp2 = 0.22), while a marginal time × group interaction was observed for serum IGF-1 (p = 0.050, ηp2 = 0.096). BFRT induced a significant increase in BDNF (mean change = 226.5 pg/mL, p = 0.006), with a greater change compared to CON (p = 0.014). IGF-1 increased significantly from baseline to 1 h post-exercise within the BFRT group (mean change = 29.2 ng/mL, p = 0.005); however, changes did not differ significantly between groups. IL-6 increased significantly following both BFRT (mean change = 8.26 pg/mL, p < 0.001) and EOE (mean change = 3.56 pg/mL, p = 0.013); however, the increase was greater only following BFRT compared to CON (p = 0.001), with no significant difference between BFRT and EOE (p = 0.123). BFRT elicited greater lactate accumulation than EOE and CON, and changes in BDNF correlated with changes in lactate (r = 0.367, p = 0.007). EOE elicited a greater CK increase than CON 48 h post-exercise, whereas syndecan-1 concentrations remained unchanged. Acute BFRT increased circulating BDNF and IGF-1 in healthy older men, and was accompanied by greater lactate accumulation, modest CK elevations, and no detectable increase in syndecan-1. The association between lactate and BDNF suggests that metabolic stress may contribute to the acute peripheral biomarker response; however, the neurological and clinical significance of these transient circulating changes remains to be established.

title: Cross-sectional associations of maladaptive sleep-hygiene behaviors with athlete engagement among provincial- and municipal-level athletes in Sichuan, China.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Maladaptive sleep-hygiene behaviors are potentially modifiable daily practices, yet their relationship with the psychological state that sustains sport involvement remains unclear. This study examined cross-sectional associations among maladaptive sleep-hygiene behaviors (MSHB), multidimensional fatigue, difficulties in emotion regulation, and athlete engagement, including three model-based indirect associations.
METHODS: A cross-sectional questionnaire survey was completed by 317 adult athletes recruited from provincial- and municipal-level teams in Sichuan Province, China. Participants represented table tennis, badminton, tennis, basketball, volleyball, and football. The Sleep Hygiene Index, the Chinese Multidimensional Fatigue Inventory, the DERS-16, and the Athlete Engagement Questionnaire were administered. A reflective partial least squares structural equation model was estimated with 5,000 bootstrap resamples. Measurement quality, construct differentiation, common-method diagnostics, out-of-sample prediction, demographic adjustment, alternative cross-sectional specifications, and subgroup robustness were evaluated.
RESULTS: More frequent MSHB were associated with greater fatigue [β = 0.491, 95% CI (0.408, 0.573)], greater difficulties in emotion regulation [β = 0.178, 95% CI (0.079, 0.274)], and lower athlete engagement [β = -0.264, 95% CI (-0.370, -0.161)]. Fatigue was associated with greater difficulties in emotion regulation [β = 0.588, 95% CI (0.500, 0.673)] and lower engagement [β = -0.325, 95% CI (-0.446, -0.205)]; difficulties in emotion regulation were also associated with lower engagement [β = -0.232, 95% CI (-0.351, -0.108)]. The total indirect association was [β = -0.268, 95% CI (-0.338, -0.204)], and the model explained 47.2% of engagement variance. Demographic adjustment yielded comparable estimates. Reverse-order and parallel specifications fitted the cross-sectional covariance structure equally well.
CONCLUSION: Within the sampled setting, more frequent MSHB co-occurred with greater fatigue, more difficulties in emotion regulation, and lower athlete engagement. Fatigue accounted for the largest specific indirect association. The single-occasion self-report design leaves actual sleep disturbance, temporal sequence, and causal effects unresolved.

title: Relationship Between Objective Measures of Sleep and Nocturnal Cardiovascular Physiology and Swimming Performance in Collegiate Female Athletes: A Bayesian Analysis.
abstract: Vatne, EA, Cencer, D, Vatne, M, Pulvermacher, K, Saenz, C, Kraemer, WJ, Robinson, B, Jones, P, Quebedeaux, N, Sprague, R, Dial, M, Carpenter, T, and Hagen, J. Relationship between objective measures of sleep and nocturnal cardiovascular physiology and swimming performance in collegiate female athletes: A Bayesian analysis. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-There is substantial evidence that sleep influences athletic performance; however, relationships with real-world competition outcomes remain unclear. Therefore, the purpose of this study was to explore the associations between objectively measured sleep, nocturnal cardiovascular physiology on the night before competition, and swim performance in female collegiate athletes. Female swimmers (n = 11) who wore a sleep monitoring device the night before competition, competed in the 200-yard freestyle (short course yard), and had ≥21 of 28 prior nights of valid data were included. Sleep metrics included total sleep time (TST), time in bed (TiB), and sleep efficiency (SE), whereas nocturnal cardiovascular metrics included heart rate variability (HRV) and resting heart rate (RHR) standardized as individualized z-scores. Race times were obtained from a publicly available database. Bayesian linear mixed-effects models estimated posterior probabilities of performance improvement. Results indicated a high probability that greater TST and TiB were associated with faster race times, with substantial support for improvements of at least 1 second per additional hour of sleep. In contrast, SE, HRV, and RHR showed low posterior evidence of meaningful associations with performance. These findings extend prior sleep and performance literature that has been confined to proxy assessments of athletic performance in controlled settings to real-world competition that should inform athlete education, emphasizing the importance of sufficient sleep opportunity and duration before competition.

title: Multidimensional Pre-Competition Stress Profiles in Wheelchair Basketball: Associations with Cortisol and Psychological Indicators.
abstract: This study examined pre-competition cortisol levels and psychological anticipation in wheelchair basketball athletes using a person-centred approach. Thirty-four male athletes (mean age: 35 ± 7.75 years) competing in a regional league provided saliva samples 35-50 min before competition and completed psychological assessments with the Revised Competitive State Anxiety Inventory-2 (CSAI-2R) and the Perceived Stress Scale. K-Means cluster analysis (k = 3), validated by Ward's hierarchical clustering (ARI = 0.947; NMI = 0.892) and Bootstrap Jaccard stability (0.544-0.603), identified three exploratory stress profiles: Low Reactor (n = 5; low cortisol, anxiety, and stress), High Reactor (n = 20; moderate cortisol, high cognitive/physical anxiety), and Physiological Stress Reactor (n = 9; high cortisol, high stress, moderate anxiety). Significant group differences were observed for log(Cortisol) (H(2) = 17.095, p < 0.001, ε2 = 0.518), Cognitive Anxiety (H(2) = 13.900, p < 0.01, ε2 = 0.421), Somatic Anxiety (H(2) = 18.840, p < 0.001, ε2 = 0.571), and Perceived Stress (H(2) = 21.831, p < 0.001, ε2 = 0.662), while self-confidence did not differ. Exploratory logistic regression indicated that functional classification, years of sport participation, match location, and match result did not significantly predict the Physiological Stress Reactor membership. These findings suggest that pre-competition stress-related characteristics may manifest in different combinations of physiological and psychological indicators. The identified profiles should be considered exploratory and require validation in larger and independent samples.

title: Is Better Diet Quality Linked to Better Competitive Functioning? An Integrative Multi-Analytic Study of Sleep Difficulty and Subjective Vitality Among Chinese Collegiate Athletes.
abstract: Background: Diet quality may be associated with recovery-related experiences and self-reported physical and psychological functioning in athletes. However, the roles of sleep difficulty and subjective vitality in these associations, together with their item-level network structure and predictive relevance, have not been examined within an integrated analytical framework. This study investigated the associations of diet quality with self-rated physical fitness and competitive psychological readiness among collegiate athletes and examined cross-sectional indirect associations involving sleep difficulty and subjective vitality. Methods: A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 1641 collegiate athletes participating in provincial-level university sporting events in Yunnan and Guizhou, China. Assessments were completed on the athletes' competition check-in day. All core variables were assessed using self-report instruments, including diet quality, sleep difficulty, subjective vitality, self-rated physical fitness, and competitive psychological readiness, with the latter operationalized using mental toughness. Cross-sectional indirect associations were estimated using PROCESS Model 6. Regularized partial-correlation networks and bridge centrality analyses were used to characterize item-level conditional associations. Ridge regression and XGBoost were further applied to evaluate out-of-sample predictive performance, and SHAP values were used to quantify the relative predictive contribution of variables within the XGBoost models. Results: Higher diet quality was significantly associated with fewer sleep difficulties and with higher subjective vitality, self-rated physical fitness, and competitive psychological readiness. Significant indirect associations were observed involving sleep difficulty alone, subjective vitality alone, and the ordered sleep difficulty-subjective vitality term in both outcome models; the subjective-vitality-only estimate was the largest. Network analysis indicated that sleep-difficulty nodes were predominantly characterized by negative bridging connections, whereas subjective-vitality nodes showed primarily positive bridging connections across communities. In the predictive analyses, Ridge regression achieved holdout R2 values of 0.415 for self-rated physical fitness and 0.341 for competitive psychological readiness. In exploratory XGBoost analyses, subjective vitality showed the highest relative SHAP importance in both models. Conclusions: Diet quality was associated with self-rated physical fitness and competitive psychological readiness, operationalized using mental toughness, with additional indirect associations involving sleep difficulty and subjective vitality. These findings provide a conceptual basis for considering nutrition, sleep, and daytime vitality within an integrated athlete-support framework. Their temporal ordering and the effects of modifying these factors require longitudinal and experimental testing.

title: Physical examination of the cervical spine should be conducted in female athletes with a history of concussion.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Female athletes may be at increased risk of injury following sports-related concussion (SRC), even after symptom resolution. Residual cervical spine impairments have been proposed as a potential contributor; however, these have not been well characterised in female athletes. This study aimed to examine whether a history of SRC was associated with clinical assessments of the cervical spine in female athletes.
METHODS: In this cross-sectional observational study, 156 elite and pre-elite female athletes from water polo, soccer, diving, rugby-7s and cycling/BMX were recruited. History of SRC within the previous 12 months was self-reported. Assessments included questionnaires and physical examination of the cervical spine, comprising range of motion, manual examination, joint position error (JPE) and maximal isometric neck strength. Between-group differences were examined using univariable statistical analyses.
RESULTS: Athletes with a history of SRC demonstrated a higher prevalence of reduced cervical range of motion, positive findings on manual examination, increased JPE and a history of headaches or migraines compared with athletes without concussion history. No deficits in maximal isometric neck strength were observed in athletes with a history of SRC.
CONCLUSION: Cervical spine impairments were more commonly observed in female athletes with a history of SRC within the previous 12 months, including in athletes who did not report current neck pain. These findings suggest consideration of targeted cervical spine assessment beyond symptom-based screening in athletes with a concussion history. Whether identification and management of cervical spine impairments influence subsequent injury risk requires investigation in prospective and interventional studies.

title: Acute Sodium Bicarbonate Supplementation Enhances 10-km Outdoor Track Running Performance in Recreational Female Runners.
abstract: This study investigated the effects of acute sodium bicarbonate (SB) supplementation co-ingested with a carbohydrate-rich meal on 10-km running performance and gastrointestinal symptoms in recreational female runners under field-based conditions. Twenty-one healthy women (33.6 ± 4.6 years; body mass index 20.8 ± 1.3 kg/m; maximal oxygen uptake 48.6 ± 2.0 ml·kg-1·min-1) completed two 10-km outdoor track running time trials (TTs) in a randomized, double-blind, crossover design. Participants ingested either SB (0.3 g/kg body mass [BM]) or placebo (PLA; 0.03 g/kg BM table salt), together with a standardized carbohydrate-rich meal (1.5 g/kg BM), 90 min before exercise during the same phase of the menstrual cycle. Blood pH, bicarbonate [HCO3-], and [lactate] were measured before, and 1, 3, 5, and 7 min after the TTs; performance time was recorded. Gastrointestinal symptoms were recorded at 30, 60, and 90 min after SB and PLA ingestions. Blood pH (7.47 ± 0.03 vs. 7.42 ± 0.04, p < .001) and [HCO3-] (27.7 ± 1.4 vs. 22.2 ± 1.5 mmol/L, p < .001) were higher at rest and remained elevated postexercise following SB compared with PLA (p < .05 for all time points). TT completion time improved after SB compared with PLA (3,046.1 ± 208.7 s vs. 3,078.4 ± 206.8 s; p = .011). No significant differences in gastrointestinal symptoms scores were observed between conditions (p > .05 for all). In conclusion, acute co-ingestion of 0.3 g/kg of SB with a carbohydrate-rich meal is a practical and well-tolerated strategy to achieve higher resting blood [HCO3-] and pH as well as to improve 10-km TT running performance in recreational female runners.

title: Arthroscopic Circumferential Labral Repair and Biceps Tenodesis in Elite Throwing Athletes: Technical Considerations.
abstract: SLAP lesions are a common cause of shoulder pain in overhead athletes and are often seen together with circumferential labral tearing, partial-thickness rotator cuff tearing, and biceps pathology. Isolated repair of the superior labrum has produced inconsistent outcomes, with low return-to-play rates in professional throwers. In patients with these complex cases, instability and anterior shoulder pain often coexist, and isolated labral repair or tenodesis may not be adequate treatment. Conversely, tenodesis without superior labral repair may increase glenohumeral translation. The senior author believes long head of the biceps tendon release reduces traction on the SLAP repair and may support healing. We describe an arthroscopic technique for circumferential labral repair, with knotless all-suture anchors performed in the beach-chair position, combined with open subpectoral biceps tenodesis and adjunct subacromial decompression. This technique restores stability, removes the biceps as a pain generator, eliminates traction on the repaired labrum, and preserves motion.

title: Extracorporeal shockwave therapy in common tendinopathies.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Extracorporeal shockwave therapy (ESWT) was initially used for urologic issues only. After Valchanou and Michailov started applying it in orthopedics in 1991, they focused on treatment of pseudarthrosis and delayed fracture healing. Some years later, shockwave therapy was also used for tendinopathies. Today, ESWT is the first-choice treatment for tendinopathies and is unsurpassed in terms of effectivity and side effects.
METHODS: This article discusses common regions of lower extremity tendinopathies (greater trochanter pain syndrome, quadriceps tendinopathy, patellar tendinopathy, Achilles tendinopathy) in a narrative review of the evidence-based literature and guidelines of leading shockwave societies such as the International Society for Medical Shockwave Treatment (ISMST) and the Deutschsprachige internationale Gesellschaft für Extrakorporale Stosswellentherapie (DIGEST). Additional case studies are also presented.
RESULTS: Extracorporeal shockwave therapy shows excellent results in the evidence-based literature and in clinical application. No other conservative treatment option in orthopedics is described as intensively in the evidence-based literature as shockwave therapy. ESWT seems to be more effective when it is accompanied by an eccentric loading/physiotherapy program.
CONCLUSION: Extracorporeal shockwave therapy enables tendon regeneration, long-term improvement, and faster return to sport, with predictable side effects and excellent tolerance.

title: Toward Wearable Joint Load Monitoring: Concurrent Estimation of Hip, Knee, and Ankle Sagittal Contact Forces from Sparse IMU Measurements.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Continuous monitoring of lower extremity joint contact forces is critical for rehabilitation medicine, sports injury prevention, and assistive device development. Yet, current wearable solutions often lack multi-joint integration or require cumbersome sensor arrays. This study aims to concurrently estimate hip, knee, and ankle sagittal compressive contact forces using a sparse inertial measurement unit (IMU) configuration across diverse daily activities.
METHODS: We collected data from 14 healthy adults equipped with four IMU sensors performing various daily movements, with reference contact forces captured using optical motion capture and force platforms. To estimate joint contact forces, we developed a domain-informed multi-task temporal convolutional network (Ada-Att-MTCN). This architecture integrates a shared temporal convolutional network encoder, task-specific attention mechanisms, homoscedastic uncertainty-based dynamic task weighting, and a soft physiological-bound penalty. Performance was evaluated using 14-fold leave-one-subject-out nested cross-validation against 4 baseline methods, with root mean square error (RMSE) and coefficient of determination (R²) as evaluation metrics.
RESULTS: On the self-collected dataset, Ada-Att-MTCN achieved the highest accuracy across all activities, with mean RMSEs of 0.328 ± 0.13 BW (hip), 0.380 ± 0.09 BW (knee), and 0.365 ± 0.15 BW (ankle), and an average R2 of 0.822 ± 0.10. On the external dataset, Ada-Att-MTCN likewise performed best among all methods (average R² = 0.754 ± 0.05).
CONCLUSION: The proposed framework captures complex inter-joint dynamics, enabling robust simultaneous load estimation with drastically reduced hardware complexity.
SIGNIFICANCE: This approach provides a practical, non-invasive solution for transitioning lab-grade multi-joint load monitoring to wearable deployment in rehabilitation and sports medicine.

title: Should athletes take omega-3 supplements? Current evidence for recovery, adaptation and performance.
abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: To evaluate whether long-chain n-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid supplementation provides meaningful benefits for recovery, training adaptation or performance in athletic populations, while distinguishing mechanistic plausibility from demonstrated functional effects.
RECENT FINDINGS: Recent data from athletic populations show that Omega-3 Index (O3I) values commonly fall below proposed cardioprotective thresholds, although athlete-specific targets remain unvalidated. Meta-analyses and controlled trials suggest that supplementation may modestly reduce muscle soreness and attenuate selected losses of muscle function following damaging exercise. However, findings are inconsistent across formulations, doses and outcomes, and benefits do not translate reliably into improved strength, endurance, power or sport performance. Evidence concerning female, masters and contact-sport athletes is limited.
SUMMARY: Routine supplementation cannot at present be recommended for all athletes. Targeted supplementation may be considered following dietary and, wherever appropriate, biomarker assessment, while recognizing that benefits during unusually damaging or congested training remain unproven.

title: Prebiotics in sport and exercise: current evidence, practical applications, and methodological considerations.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Prebiotics are selectively utilized by the host microbiota and can confer health and/or performance benefits, in part through increasing the abundance of beneficial gut microorganisms and their metabolites. While several studies have shown promising initial findings, high-quality scientific evidence examining the effects of prebiotics on athlete performance, health and wellbeing remains limited.
METHODS: This narrative review summarizes the current available evidence on prebiotic intake in athletic populations, including effects on gastrointestinal structure and function, immune responses, recovery, sleep, wellness, mood and exercise performance. In areas where there is limited evidence in athletic cohorts, but a physiological rationale for a benefit, findings from sedentary and/or clinical populations are evaluated, and the potential relevance of these findings to athletes are discussed. Finally, considerations for practitioners around the use of prebiotics with athletes are provided, and recommendations for designing future prebiotic-based research are explored.
RESULTS: Despite the limited existing literature around prebiotic use in athletes, there are several studies that indicate their potential to improve gut barrier integrity and reduce the incidence/severity of gastrointestinal symptoms. Data also indicates that prebiotics can increase salivary Immunoglobulin A secretion rate and reduce the duration and/or severity of upper respiratory symptoms in trained individuals. Other areas with emerging evidence that warrant further investigation in athletic populations include prebiotics' ability to support exercise adaptation and recovery, promote sleep improvements and enhance mood and cognitive function. The interpretation of current studies is limited by the lack of gut microbiome and metabolome measures and the absence of robust performance measures following a period of prebiotic supplementation. Well-controlled, adequately powered studies incorporating these outcomes are needed to determine the contexts in which prebiotic intake can meaningfully improve health and performance metrics, and to elucidate the underlying physiological mechanisms of any beneficial effects.
CONCLUSION: Prebiotic intake represents a promising intervention to attenuate exercise-induced disturbances to the intestinal epithelium, reduce exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptoms, and lower the duration/severity of upper respiratory symptoms in athletes. Future studies should prioritize high-quality performance assessments, alongside comprehensive microbiome and metabolome profiling, to elucidate mechanistic effects. Areas with limited current evidence such as recovery, sleep, mood, cognitive function, bone health and nutrient absorption in athlete cohorts should also be further explored.

title: Core Muscle Injury: A Combined Orthopaedic and General Surgery Algorithmic Approach for Diagnosis, Imaging, and Treatment.
abstract: » Core muscle injury (CMI) is a common cause of groin pain in athletes and reflects pathology of the inguinal canal, rectus abdominis-adductor longus (RA-AL) aponeurosis, and pubic symphysis. » There is a substantial lack of consensus on terminology and diagnostic criteria for CMI, hindering standardized evaluation, management, and research initiatives. » Diagnosis relies on structured history, physical examinations, and provocative maneuvers to identify CMI and concurrent pathology, and fluid-sensitive pelvic magnetic resonance imaging to characterize RA-AL injury. » Treatment strategies differ across sports medicine physicians, general surgeons, and orthopaedic surgeons, underscoring the need for early cross-departmental referrals to ensure all contributing pathologies are comprehensively identified and addressed. » When both adductor/RA-AL aponeurosis and inguinal canal/abdominal wall pathologies are present, prioritizing collaborative cases between orthopaedic and general surgeons is essential for decreasing operating room time, streamlining rehabilitation, and optimizing return-to-sport outcomes.

title: Imaging of acute sports injuries of the shoulder girdle.
abstract: Acute injuries of the shoulder girdle commonly result from sports activities and lead to imaging studies. Radiologists who interpret these studies should be familiar with traumatic mechanisms and the imaging manifestations of glenohumeral dislocation, acromioclavicular sprain, rotator cuff tear, labral tear, osseous contusion or fracture, and myotendinous strain. Imaging findings are crucial for making accurate diagnoses, grading the severity of injuries, guiding treatment plans, and managing the athletes' expectations for rehabilitation and return to sport. In this review article, we address common and uncommon injuries in both young and mature athletes. Focusing on magnetic resonance imaging, we provide examples of classic injuries and discuss pitfalls that challenge diagnostic interpretation.

title: Advanced Footwear Technology in Distance Running: What We Know, What We Don't Know, and Future Directions.
abstract: Over the past decade, running shoes have undergone substantial innovation with the emergence of Advanced Footwear Technology (AFT). Shoes with AFT are typically characterized by highly compliant (deformable) and resilient (high energy return) midsole foams, embedded curved stiffening elements, low mass, and a rockered longitudinal geometry. This expert statement aims to synthesize established knowledge, remaining uncertainties and key directions for future research on AFT in middle- and long-distance running. Current literature demonstrates robust improvements in running economy and performance with AFT, with reported metabolic savings of approximately 2%-4%, and corresponding performance improvements of 1%-3%. These benefits likely arise from a combination of "acute" and possibly "long-term" mechanisms. Proposed acute mechanisms include decreased muscle force production due to higher positive work from energy-returning foams, lower muscle force production to accommodate mechanical running demands due to compliant midsoles, and improved mechanical efficiency associated with greater longitudinal bending stiffness and curved geometry. Importantly, AFT features have a synergistic effect, with the relative importance of each mechanism differing depending on the context. Emerging evidence also suggests potential reductions in muscle damage/inflammation and soreness, which could support better physiological resilience, and higher training volumes/quality. From a biomechanical injury risk perspective, AFT can redistribute loading, potentially increasing metatarsal and tarsal stress while reducing tibia and possibly Achilles tendon loading. However, injury risk associated with AFT use remains equivocal, with limited high-quality data. Notably, substantial inter-individual variability has been observed, influencing both running economy and potential injury risk although the determinants of this variability remain unclear.

title: Exploring the Impact of Ovarian Hormones on Cortical Drive and Quadriceps Performance in Uninjured Female Athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Ovarian hormones fluctuate across the menstrual cycle (MC) and differ between oral contraceptive (OC) users and naturally menstruating (NM) individuals. Hormones may affect cortical drive to peripheral muscles through excitatory effects of estradiol and inhibitory effects of progesterone on the central nervous system. The impact of hormones on cortical drive is poorly understood. This study aimed to (1) determine the effects of MC phase and OC use on cortical drive and quadriceps performance and (2) determine the relationship between ovarian hormones and these outcomes. We hypothesized that cortical drive will differ between MC phases in NM individuals but not in OC users. Cortical drive will be positively associated with circulating estradiol.
METHODS: Fourteen NM individuals and 11 OC users completed two time points (high hormone: NM mid-luteal, OC active pill and low hormone: NM early follicular, OC placebo). Hormone concentrations were quantified using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays. Quadriceps performance (isometric peak torque [PTISOM] and rate of torque development) was measured using an isokinetic dynamometer. Corticospinal excitability and intracortical excitability (short-interval intracortical inhibition [SICI] and intracortical facilitation) were assessed using transcranial magnetic stimulation. Linear mixed-effect models were used to examine hormone status, phase, and interaction effects. Linear regression determined associations between hormones, cortical drive, and strength.
RESULTS: There were no significant main effects or interactions for any cortical drive measure. There was a phase by hormone status interaction on the rate of torque development from 0 to 100 ms (RTD100), with a greater RTD100 at the high hormone phase than at the low hormone phase in the NM group but no difference between time points in the OC group. There was a main effect of phase on PTISOM, with a greater PTISOM at the low hormone phase regardless of hormone status. SICI was negatively associated with estradiol. RTD100 was positively associated with progesterone and moderated by hormone status.
CONCLUSIONS: MC phase did not impact cortical drive but did impact quadriceps performance. There were between-phase differences in speed of contraction among NM individuals but not among OC users. A higher progesterone level was associated with faster speed of contraction, especially among NM participants.
KEY CONCEPTS: (1)Corticospinal and intracortical excitability did not differ by menstrual cycle (MC) phase or oral contraceptive (OC) use.(2)Quadriceps rate of torque development was associated with progesterone concentration and varied across the MC, suggesting hormone expression influenced the rate of torque development (RTD) (speed of contraction).(3)The influence of endogenous ovarian hormones on RTD (speed of contraction) differed between OC users and naturally menstruating individuals.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: II.

title: Facilitators and Barriers to Treatment Access and Use in Black Individuals With Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury: A Qualitative Study.
abstract:
CONTEXT: Individuals with anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury are at high risk of knee osteoarthritis. Black individuals with osteoarthritis have worse pain and disability than White individuals. Racial disparities in ACL treatment use (ACL reconstruction and physical therapy) may contribute to disparities in long-term osteoarthritis-related disability. However, factors influencing ACL injury disparities are unknown. We explored facilitators and barriers to treatment access and use in Black individuals with ACL injury.
DESIGN: Qualitative (semistructured interviews).
METHODS: We included Black or African American individuals who self-reported ACL injury up to 5 years prior to recruitment, no longer seeking care for the injury, and 16-50 years old. We conducted one-on-one semistructured interviews and topics included facilitators and barriers to care, perceived communication, medical trust, and perceived discrimination. We used a reflexive thematic analysis approach to analyze the interviews.
RESULTS: We included 10 participants (age 21-49 y, 8 women). We generated 4 themes: (1) path to diagnosis, (2) patient approach to treatment, (3) patient-provider interactions, and (4) life demands. ACL injury recovery was often complex with frustrations particularly common during the diagnosis process due to lack of an accurate diagnosis and poor communication on next steps. Participants took various approaches to treatment use including active, passive, and more autonomous approaches. Family obligations and transportation barriers posed challenges to accessing treatment. Lack of health insurance was a barrier affecting multiple aspects of recovery. Participants often desired shared decision making. Several types of perceived discrimination were discussed including race, gender, insurance, and weight. Facilitators were often related to positive communication or athletic program resources.
CONCLUSION: Facilitators included shared decision making, provider empathy and encouragement, and athletic program resources. Barriers included a lack of listening to patients' concerns, lack of health insurance, transportation challenges, and perceived discrimination.

title: Post-Exercise Thermal Interventions and Nocturnal Sleep in Athletes: A Narrative Review of the Potential Underlying Physiological Mechanisms.
abstract: Sleep is essential for optimal performance and recovery in athletes. Post-exercise cold exposure, including cold water immersion and cryotherapy, is typically used to enhance recovery, but its effects on sleep remain unclear. Emerging evidence also suggests that post-exercise heat exposure, including sauna and hot water immersion before sleep may improve both objective and subjective sleep outcomes. However, the effectiveness of post-exercise thermal interventions for improving nocturnal sleep in athletes specifically has not yet been comprehensively evaluated. This narrative review synthesizes the current evidence and discusses the potential physiological mechanisms by which post-exercise thermal interventions may influence nocturnal sleep in athletes. Despite methodological heterogeneity, existing research indicates that post-exercise thermal interventions may influence the subsequent nocturnal sleep of athletes through multiple and varying interacting mechanisms. For example, cold exposure close to bedtime (< 2 h) may disrupt sleep by reducing the distal-to-proximal skin temperature gradient (DPG), thereby increasing sleep onset latency and shortening sleep duration. In contrast, when applied more than 2 h before bedtime, cold exposure may improve sleep by augmenting parasympathetic tone and/or reducing muscle soreness and associated nocturnal movement. Although it remains unclear whether post-exercise heat exposure improves sleep via autonomic modulation or reduced muscle soreness, existing evidence indicates that sleep may be facilitated by an increased DPG. Moderating factors such as sex, time of day, environmental temperature, bedding microclimate, acclimatization status, and training load may influence the effects of post-exercise thermal interventions on sleep and should be investigated in future studies.

title: Effect of Pulsed Electromagnetic Stimulation on Delayed Onset Muscle Soreness: Randomized Sham-Controlled Trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The effect of pulsed electromagnetic field (PEMF) therapy on muscle performance and serum creatine kinase (CK) and myoglobin (Mb) values - the biomarkers of muscle damage in experimentally induced delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS) - has yet to be investigated. PEMF therapy is known to be effective to reduce muscle pain, muscle recovery time, fatigue but not to increase muscle force production. The study aimed to compare the effect of PEMF and sham therapy on experimentally induced DOMS in sedentary undergraduate college students.
HYPOTHESIS: PEMF therapy would improve pain, pressure pain threshold (PPT), functional performance, serum CK activity, and Mb concentration compared with the sham intervention.
STUDY DESIGN: Randomized, participant- and assessor-blinded, sham-controlled study.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 2.
METHODS: This study was conducted at Pamukkale University Sarayköy Vocational School. A total of 52 healthy sedentary people received 3 consecutive days of active (Experimental group, n = 26) or sham (Sham group, n = 26) PEMF therapy 24 hours after DOMS induction with a drop-jump protocol. Pain intensity, PPT, functional performance, serum CK activity, and Mb concentration were assessed at baseline, 24 hours and 72 hours after DOMS induction protocol.
RESULTS: The drop-jump protocol induced DOMS successfully in both groups (P < 0.05). All outcome measures were improved in the experimental group (P < 0.05). Mean change scores of PPT (P = 0.53), functional performance (P = 0.10), serum CK (P = 0.38), and Mb concentrations (P = 0.08) were not significantly different between baseline and 72 hours in the sham group. Statistically significant decreases in Mb concentrations were determined in the sham group (P = 0.001).
CONCLUSION: Compared with sham, PEMF therapy improved pain, PPT, functional performance, serum CK activity, and Mb concentration. The duration of PEMF therapy was sufficient to resolve the PPT, functional performance, and serum CK and Mb concentrations associated with DOMS.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This study adds to existing knowledge in showing that, compared with sham, PEMF therapy improved pain, PPT, functional performance, serum CK activity, and Mb concentration.

title: A Translational Approach for Treatment of Posterior Cruciate Ligament Injuries: From Foundational Anatomic and Biomechanical Studies to Validated Surgical Outcomes.
abstract: Posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) injuries were historically managed nonsurgically or with primary repairs, owing to limited anatomic knowledge, subjective diagnostic techniques, and nonvalidated reconstructions that frequently failed. We describe a two-decade, bench-to-bedside PCL research pyramid that progressively addressed these deficiencies. Foundational cadaveric work characterized the quantitative anatomy of the PCL, including the anterolateral and posteromedial bundles, yielding reproducible femoral and tibial osseous landmarks for tunnel placement. Robotic biomechanical testing established the codominant contribution of both bundles, optimal graft fixation angles, and the destabilizing influence of posterolateral corner injuries and flat tibial slope. Objective diagnostic methods, such as kneeling PCL stress radiography and posterior tibial translation on MRI, were validated to quantify laxity and detect chronic tears. These insights informed an anatomically grounded double-bundle reconstruction, complemented by multiligament tunnel convergence-avoidance strategies, evidence-based tensioning sequences, and a refined rehabilitation and bracing treatment protocol. Prospective outcome studies confirmed restoration of stability comparable to anterior cruciate ligament reconstructions, demonstrating how integrated translational research transformed treatment of this challenging injury.

title: Transient ST-T Changes During Submaximal Exercise Revealing Anomalous Right Coronary Artery Origin in an Asymptomatic Athlete.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Anomalous aortic origin of a coronary artery is a recognised structural cause of sudden cardiac death in athletes younger than 35 years. Most affected individuals are asymptomatic prior to cardiac events, and resting and exercise electrocardiography (ECG) findings are frequently normal or non-specific, limiting the effectiveness of preparticipation screening.
CASE SUMMARY: We report a case of a 22-year-old asymptomatic athlete in whom preparticipation screening revealed transient ST-segment depression and T-wave inversions during submaximal exercise and recovery, whereas findings at peak exercise remained normal. Point-of-care echocardiography performed by a sports medicine specialist raised suspicion of an anomalous origin of the right coronary artery from the left aortic sinus of Valsalva, which was subsequently confirmed by computed tomography coronary angiography. High-risk anatomical features included an acute ostial angle and an interarterial course of the right coronary artery. Functional testing with exercise myocardial stress scintigraphy showed no inducible perfusion defect. Following multidisciplinary consultation, a conservative management strategy with activity modification and close follow-up was adopted.
DISCUSSION: This case highlights the potential clinical significance of transient ST-T abnormalities occurring during submaximal exercise and recovery, even in the absence of symptoms or abnormalities at peak workload. In this patient, recognition of this reproducible but non-specific ECG pattern prompted further structural evaluation leading to the diagnosis of AAOCA. It also underscores the limitations of current guidelines in managing asymptomatic athletes with high-risk coronary anatomy but without evidence of inducible ischaemia, supporting the need for individualised decision-making.

title: Bilateral erector spinae and biceps femoris co-activation following unilateral hamstring injury in young sprinters.
abstract: This study compared coactivation and strength of the erector spinae (ES) and biceps femoris long head (BFLH) during isometric knee flexion and trunk extension in sprinters with a recent BFLH injury. Twenty-four sprinters with grade 2 BFLH injury and 21 controls performed prone trunk extension and knee flexion maximal voluntary contractions (MVCs) at 90° and 0° knee flexion. Torque and surface electromyography (EMG) of the ES and BFLH were recorded bilaterally and normalized to MVCs during 30° trunk extension and 0° knee flexion, respectively. Previously injured athletes showed a greater co-contraction index (CCI) during knee flexion at 0° and 90° than controls (p < 0.001), with higher ES activation (32.52 ± 17.08 to 47.72 ± 17.83% MVC) than the uninjured group (21.56 ± 14.52 to 44.68 ± 18.02% MVC; p < 0.05). No group differences were found in normalized BFLH EMG, CCI during trunk extension, or absolute knee flexion or trunk extension strength (p > 0.05). Previously injured sprinters showed larger between-limb knee flexion strength asymmetries (>10%, p < 0.01), which were absent in controls. This paraspinal overactivation and increased trunk-hamstring co-contraction after BFLH injury suggest that lumbopelvic control exercises may be beneficial for preventing BFLH re-injury.

title: Shoulder Instability Pediatric Management of Shoulder Instability in the Pediatric Athlete: A Contemporary Review of Current Evidence.
abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Shoulder instability in pediatric and adolescent athletes is increasingly common and clinically complex due to early sport specialization and high-demand participation. This review aims to inform clinical decision-making by synthesizing contemporary evidence on injury patterns, diagnostic techniques, treatment options, and associated outcomes when faced with treating pediatric athletes.
RECENT FINDINGS: Unique anatomic and developmental features specific to the pediatric population including capsular elasticity, collagen composition, open physes, and evolving glenoid and humeral morphology contribute to age-specific injury patterns and influence treatment outcomes. Younger children more frequently sustain atypical soft-tissue lesions, while adolescents experience markedly higher recurrence risk with rates of 44-77% following nonoperative management. Adolescents also develop off-track Hill-Sachs lesions more frequently than adults (24.4% vs. 3.3%), reflecting differences in immature bone mechanics. Diagnosis requires thorough history, physical examination, assessment of social and socioeconomic factors, and advanced imaging. Arthroscopic Bankart repair remains the most common surgical intervention and yields high return to sport rates (75-90%), though recurrence in pediatric patients (15-50%) substantially exceeds adult rates. Remplissage reduces recurrence in adolescents with off-track lesions, and bone augmentation procedures such as the Latarjet demonstrate lower recurrence (3-8%) in patients with significant glenoid bone loss or failed prior stabilization. Long-term outcomes in skeletally immature patients and alternative bone block procedures remain incompletely studied. Management requires individualized risk stratification based on adherence, skeletal maturity, sport demands, bone loss, lesion morphology and patient history and adherence. Although surgical stabilization provides favorable functional outcomes and high return to sport rates, recurrence remains a significant concern in younger and collision-sport athletes.

title: The effect of positive emotions on psychophysiological recovery and performance in athletes - investigating the undoing-hypothesis.
abstract: Athletes have to cope with psychosocial and physiological stressors, requiring recovery to ensure subsequent performance. According to the undoing-hypothesis, positive emotions (PE) may enhance psychophysiological recovery. The present two studies investigated the undoing hypothesis and its benefits for athletes' cognitive (Study 1; n = 60) and motor (Study 2; n = 30) performance. After a combined psychosocial-physiological stressor, participants either completed a five-minute PE induction (music; imagination exercise) or were assigned to a resting condition. Emotions, perceived stress-recovery, and physiological parameters (e.g., heart rate, heart rate variability, cortisol) were assessed. In Study 1, inhibition and cognitive flexibility were measured once. In Study 2, hand force and jump height were measured using a pre-posttest design. Due to the lack of psychological stress responses and successful PE induction, no conclusions could be drawn regarding the undoing hypothesis. Nevertheless, the present study provides valuable methodological insights into the challenges of testing the undoing hypothesis in athletes. These insights can inform the design and implementation of future studies and thereby contribute to advancing research on the undoing hypothesis in athletic populations.

title: Bilateral Lower-Body Force Asymmetry and Countermovement Jump Performance of South African Amateur Padel Athletes.
abstract: The countermovement jump (CMJ) is a widely used assessment of lower-limb power and neuromuscular function. The physical demands of padel, including repeated accelerations, decelerations, changes of direction, jumping, and landing, may contribute to inter-limb asymmetries influencing performance and injury risk. This quantitative cross-sectional study investigated lower-limb asymmetries during the CMJ in amateur (non-professional) padel athletes. Thirty participants (mean age: 41.2 ± 14.5 years; 63% male, 37% female) completed bilateral CMJ assessments using VALD (Brisbane, Australia) ForceDecks force plates. Outcome measures included concentric, eccentric, and landing peak force, peak power, rate of force development and jump height. Significant dominant-limb advantages were identified for concentric (p = 0.002), eccentric (p = 0.024), and landing peak force (p = 0.044). Male athletes demonstrated greater jump heights than female athletes (p < 0.001), while female athletes exhibited greater landing-phase force asymmetry (p = 0.004). Amateur padel athletes display significant inter-limb asymmetries in force production across the concentric, eccentric, and landing phases of the CMJ, with greater force generation in the dominant limb. Furthermore, the greater landing asymmetry observed in female athletes may reflect reduced inter-limb load distribution during landing tasks. These results highlight the value of CMJ assessment in identifying neuromuscular asymmetries that may influence performance and increase injury risk in padel athletes.

title: Concussion symptom clusters and changes in symptom reporting and severity following multiple concussions in male professional rugby league players.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Symptom reporting remains an important part of the diagnosis and management of concussion. Understanding the patterns of symptoms and symptom clusters in athletes with multiple concussions may be clinically valuable. The purpose of this study was to characterise acute symptom reporting in players with multiple concussions.
METHODS: National Rugby League (NRL) players who have sustained multiple concussions between the 2017 and 2022 seasons were included in the study. Data included the symptoms reported on the Sport Concussion Assessment Tool - 5th Edition (SCAT5) during the Head Injury Assessment by players who were subsequently diagnosed with concussion. K-means clustering with k = 6 centres was performed on symptom severity data. Each concussion episode was assigned to one symptom cluster based on the athlete's symptom presentation. Transitions between symptom clusters from initial to subsequent concussions were visualised using a Sankey plot.
RESULTS: There were 120 players who sustained more than one concussion, including 75 players with two, 23 with three, 15 with four, and 7 players with five or more medically diagnosed concussions. The average duration between concussions was 441 days (SD: 332; Md: 370; range: 11-1435 days). There were 6 different symptom clusters identified. Players were commonly found to transition between clusters for subsequent concussions, most commonly the 'Asymptomatic' cluster. There was no relationship found for days between concussions and symptom count or severity. Symptom severity, but not symptom count, was associated with days until medical clearance.
CONCLUSION: Acute symptom reporting varies with subsequent concussions, making it difficult to predict post-concussion symptoms in individual players. Acute symptom severity was associated with time to medical clearance, whereas the number of concussions in the preceding two years was not.

title: Exercise Is Associated with Skeletal Muscle Autophagy-Lysosome-Related Markers and Nrf2/ARF1 Signaling in HFD Mice.
abstract: Purpose: This study aimed to investigate the protective effects and potential mechanisms of exercise against long-term high-fat diet (HFD)-induced skeletal muscle dysfunction, with a focus on ADP-ribosylation factor 1 (ARF1)-related autophagy-lysosome markers and nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) signaling. Methods: Forty male C57BL/6 mice were randomly divided into a normal diet group (DC) and an HFD group, and the latter was further subdivided into a model group (MG), exercise group (EG), Nrf2 inhibitor group (NG), and exercise combined with Nrf2 inhibitor group (ENG) after 12 weeks of HFD feeding. EG received 6 weeks of moderate-intensity treadmill exercise, NG was treated with Nrf2 inhibitor for 6 weeks, and ENG received both the 6-week treadmill exercise and inhibitor injections simultaneously. Serum lipid, blood glucose and insulin resistance indices were detected; skeletal muscle morphology was observed by H&E staining; mRNA and protein expression of ARF1, ULK1, ATP6V0A1 and other factors were determined by RT-qPCR, Western blotting and immunohistochemistry; the oxidative stress index was measured by an ELISA; and the colocalization of ARF1/ATP6V0A1 with the lysosomal marker Lamp1 was analyzed by immunofluorescence. Results: Long-term HFD significantly increased mouse body weight, serum TC, TG, LDL-C, FBG levels and the HOMA-IR index, induced morphological alterations in skeletal muscle (loose myofiber arrangement, abundant intracellular vacuoles), inhibited the mRNA expression of ARF1, ULK1 and ATP6V0A1, and elevated malondialdehyde (MDA) content (p < 0.05 or p < 0.01). Six weeks of moderate-intensity treadmill exercise effectively improved HFD-induced metabolic disorders and skeletal muscle morphological damage, upregulated the expression of ARF1, ULK1 and ATP6V0A1, and reduced oxidative stress (p < 0.05 or p < 0.01). Notably, luteolin-mediated inhibition of Nrf2 signaling may partially reverse exercise-induced alterations in ARF1-related autophagy-lysosome markers and skeletal muscle morphology. Conclusions: Long-term HFD may induce morphological alterations in skeletal muscle, accompanied by changes in ARF1-associated autophagy-lysosome markers and elevated oxidative stress. Conversely, moderate-intensity exercise may ameliorate HFD-related changes in skeletal muscle morphology, potentially via Nrf2 signaling, providing a potential molecular target and theoretical basis for the exercise intervention strategies against HFD-induced metabolic-related skeletal muscle dysfunction.

title: Effects of muscle length and age on neuromuscular responses to maximal eccentric contractions of the plantar flexors.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Eccentric contractions induce greater neuromuscular impairment and muscle damage than concentric contractions. Muscle length is a key modulator of these responses, yet the combined effects of eccentric contractions and muscle length on neuromuscular function in older adults remain unclear. We investigated acute and delayed neuromuscular responses to eccentric plantar flexor contractions performed at different muscle lengths in young and older adults.
METHODS: Twenty-four young and 26 older adults performed 10 sets of 10 maximal eccentric plantar flexor contractions at either short (30°-0° plantar flexion) or long (0°-30° dorsiflexion) muscle lengths (12 young and 13 older adults per condition). Maximal voluntary isometric contraction, voluntary activation, and evoked responses (100 Hz and 10 Hz doublets) were measured before, immediately after, and 1, 24, and 48 h post-exercise. Changes were compared between groups and conditions.
RESULTS: Despite similar torque-time integrals between young and older adults within the same muscle length condition, a muscle length effect was only found in young adults, with a greater (p = 0.021) MVIC decrease at long (-33.6 ± 13.2%) than short lengths (-8.4 ± 15.7%). Older adults showed similar reductions across conditions (≈ - 14-21%). Voluntary activation decreased only at long lengths, with no age difference. Evoked responses showed an age effect (p = 0.032), and the 10/100 Hz ratio decreased only in young after long muscle lengths. Neuromuscular function returned to baseline within 24 h indicating no evidence of severe alteration, although muscle soreness remained elevated at 48 h.
CONCLUSION: Long muscle length eccentric contractions induced greater force loss in young but not older adults, with no evidence of prolonged functional impairment in healthy, physically active older adults.

title: Creative Solution for Recurrent Failure of Flexor Tendon Repair.
abstract: Flexor tendon injuries present complex surgical and rehabilitative challenges, particularly in zone 2 of the hand. This article presents a case of recurrent flexor tendon failure in a young manual laborer, detailing initial repair, rupture, and secondary reconstruction. Despite multiple complications, including recurrent ruptures and repair failures, the case underscores the importance of individualized surgical planning, coordinated rehabilitation, and shared decision-making in achieving optimal functional recovery.

title: Investigational Peptides in Orthopaedic Practice: Evidence, Safety, and Patient Counseling for BPC-157, Thymosin Beta-4, and TB-500.
abstract: Peptide-based products, particularly Body Protection Compound-157 (BPC-157), and thymosin beta-4 (TB-4), and products marketed as TB-500, are increasingly promoted for musculoskeletal recovery despite limited clinical validation. This narrative review evaluated their molecular rationale, direct musculoskeletal evidence, human safety and efficacy data, product quality concerns, regulatory status, antidoping implications, and relevance to orthopaedic counseling. PubMed/MEDLINE, EMBASE, and Scopus were searched from inception through June 2026, with additional review of primary regulatory and antidoping sources. BPC-157 has the largest bod of direct musculoskeletal preclinical evidence, including predominantly small-animal studies involving tendon, ligament, muscle, inflammatory joint disease, and bone. However, human musculoskeletal evidence is limited to one small retrospective uncontrolled case series without validated outcome measures. Validated dosing, pharmacokinetic, and long-term safety data are lacking. TB-4 has broader experimental and human experience in ophthalmic, dermatologic, and cardiovascular applications, but direct musculoskeletal evidence remains limited to in vitro and rodent studies. These nonorthopaedic findings cannot establish musculoskeletal efficacy or safety. TB-500 is a distinct seven amino-acid fragment of TB-4 that is frequently conflated with full-length TB-4 despite the absence of validated biologic or clinical equivalence. Commercial products marketed also raise concerns regarding identity, purity, concentration, sterility, and manufacturing consistency. None of these agents has an FDA-approved musculoskeletal indication, validated orthopaedic treatment protocol, or controlled human orthopaedic efficacy evidence. Orthopaedic clinicians should specifically ask about peptide use, distinguish preclinical plausibility from clinical validation, address product quality and safety uncertainties, and counsel athletes regarding antidoping restrictions. Routine clinical use cannot be currently recommended.

title: Baseline Symptom Collection in Elite Rugby Union Players-Limited Clinical Utility? An Investigation of Assessments Across 5879 men and Women Athletes.
abstract: In World Rugby's Head Injury Assessment (HIA) protocol, a modified Sports Concussion Assessment Tool (SCAT) is completed during the pre-season (baseline) and when a player has a suspected head injury. The symptom component of the SCAT, which involves comparing current to baseline symptoms, has been shown to be the most predictive component for concussion diagnosis. Because the clinical comparison of symptom report to baseline is a key determinant of concussion diagnosis, this study aims to explore the relationship between symptoms endorsement at baseline and during HIA. Mean and standard deviation (SD) or median and interquartile ranges (IQR) are presented along with relevant bivariate analyses. Logistic regressions compared proportions of symptom endorsement profiles between men and women. At baseline, 'Trouble sleeping' and 'Fatigue or low energy' were commonly reported symptoms for men and women. At baseline, women (mean + SD) reported more symptoms than men (mean + SD) on average. During the HIA, women players were nearly 3 times (Relative risk: 2.98 95% CIs: 2.47-3.60) more likely than men to report fewer symptoms immediately after the match than at baseline (47% women vs. 16% men). While this study highlights the importance of collecting baseline assessment as a medical overview of players, it de-emphasises the relevance of baseline symptoms when using the SCAT as a clinical assessment tool in professional rugby players. This study also highlights important differences in men and women's rugby players in symptom reporting, and recommends de-coupling baseline symptom reporting from the diagnostic part of the HIA.

title: A two-factor framework to assess international male field hockey movement characteristics: Implications for performance preparation.
abstract: We aimed to establish the nature and structure of the relationships between high-intensity movement characteristics during international field hockey matches. Global positioning system data were obtained from 28 elite male field hockey players (n = 393 international player-matches). Mean and 90% trimmed range were extracted for the 10 most intense 1-min periods (separated by >60s) for: total distance (m); high-speed distance (>5 m·s-1); sprint distance (>7 m·s-1); accelerations (>2.5 m·s-2); decelerations (<-2.5 m·s-2) and high-speed cuts (>45° change-of-direction at >5 m·s-1). Pearson's correlations were calculated for pairs of characteristics (summed across the 10 most intense periods). An exploratory factor analysis was then applied to movement characteristics. Finally, factors were validated by testing whether they discriminated between playing positions using random-effect linear-mixed models. Factor analysis explained 76% of total variance (χ42 = 286, p < 0.001) and resulted in a two-factor solution: 'Distance' (total, high-speed and sprint distance), and 'Acceleration' (accelerations and decelerations). High-speed cuts loaded onto both factors. The two factors also discriminated significantly between playing positions. Our data-driven approach indicates that Distance and Acceleration are distinct factors of international male field hockey, specifically, Midfielders cover more distance than Defenders, and Strikers change speed and direction more than Midfielders or Defenders. Practitioners should consider prescribing and monitoring these distinct factors separately.
